entry.title: Lord of Bench Is Fighting for Your Right to Sit

div.p: A plaza just outside 780 Third Avenue in Midtown Manhattan, brimming with well-tended flowers in warm weather and furnished with elegant stone benches, looks like an inviting place to sit down and enjoy a slice of pizza. Or at least Wade Phillips certainly thought so.

Phillips, a hospitality and security worker, used to take his breaks in that plaza every day. (“Wade Phillips” isn’t his real name, but a nom de guerre, or what its user refers to as “my please-don’t-fire-me name”). He describes himself as “kind of a Good Will Hunting guy,” referring to the Matt Damon character in Gus Van Sant’s 1997 movie about a self-taught working-class genius who has survived an abusive childhood. “I don’t really have a family,” says Phillips, “I’ve had kind of a rough road.”

For the past few decades, working in Manhattan, sometimes living with roommates, parks like this have been a respite where he’s been grateful to “go sit somewhere and breathe.” Such spaces provide a sense of peace for free for anyone who needs to rest a spell.

Last year, he was working on Forty-Eighth Street, taking his breaks almost every day on a bench in the especially idyllic plaza at 780 Third Avenue. “From the day I had my interview there,” he says, “till the day I left, it was, like, my spot.” On one occasion, Phillips had been having a rough night at work, and it was the anniversary of his father’s death. He needed some time to himself on the bench. A security guard appeared immediately and told Phillips he couldn’t be there. “I just need ten minutes,” Phillips told the guard, who was unmoved and insisted he move along.
Grumpily acceding to the guard’s demand, Philips crossed the street and saw an enormous sign carved into the stone bench in question. It read, “Welcome.”
“Everyone has their breaking point,” he says, “and that was it for me.” Phillips emphasized, “It doesn’t just say ‘Welcome.’ It’s carved in.” That moment, he says, is “when this whole thing started.”

Phillips, a meticulous and detail-oriented researcher who majored in finance in college, hit the city records and learned that the public has a legal right to use that space. 780 Third Avenue and nearly six hundred other spaces like it in New York City have a somewhat complicated legal status: they are POPS, or “privately owned public spaces.”

In Midtown Manhattan especially, real estate developers often, in order to be able to add height to their building that is outside what the zoning laws would typically permit for that neighborhood, reach an agreement with the city to “trade floor space in the sky for floor space down below,” as Philips explains. Buildings may also provide POPS in exchange for other types of zoning variances, but in Midtown, height is the most common. Individual agreements vary, but they all specify the building’s obligations to the public: exact square footage; whether the owner must provide chairs, tables, or benches for public use; whether there must be trees or plants.

Privately owned public spaces throughout New York City comprise more than 3.8 million square feet of space for public leisure. The practice of allowing developers to skirt some zoning rules in exchange for providing public space has been around since 1961, but in 2017, New York City Council passed Local Law 116 to strengthen the city’s oversight of these agreements, requiring annual reporting on the POPS by the relevant agencies — the Department of Buildings and Department of City Planning — and, crucially, requiring signage indicating that the public has access to the area.

But POPS violations, in which the public are denied access to these spaces by the companies who received the legal clearance to build additional floors, are common. Much of the real estate industry bitterly resents having to provide any public goods despite having legally agreed to do so. They prefer to take up space in our skies without providing anything in return.

Phillips, particularly incensed after carrying out his legal research and learning he was in the right to sit on the bench, went back to 780 Third Avenue the next day and told the security guard that the plaza was a public park. He says the building employee insulted him and threatened to have him arrested. “I was like, ‘Okay, game on.’”

Phillips filmed these interactions and gave the guard many opportunities to change his tune before finally going live with the whole imbroglio. Thus was born the Instagram account @780_lord_of_bench, which now has 64.7K followers, including Joe Rogan and Sarah Jessica Parker. And more importantly, ordinary New Yorkers, who now file complaints about POPS abuses, attend Phillips’s celebratory POPS events — part protest, part party, calling attention to the right to public leisure in those spaces — and donate to his Patreon to support his advocacy.

He now monitors POPS throughout Midtown. On a beautiful October evening, I meet Phillips just across the street from Radio City Music Hall for a tour of some of offending properties along Sixth Avenue and an introduction to some of the notorious security regimes featured in his videos.

The outdoor tables of a restaurant, Double Knot, protrude — illegally, according to Phillips — onto the POPS at 1251 Sixth Avenue, managed by the Hines Group and owned by Mitsui Fudosan America, a real estate developer that continues to dodge a fine despite public complaints and a violation issued by the city for allowing a restaurant in a place designated as a public plaza with obvious signage.

div.p: Nearby, at 1221 Sixth, property of The Rockefeller Group, which owns and manages some six million square feet of office space in Midtown Manhattan, a sunken plaza — also a POPS — has at times been blocked off on weekends. Due to complaints and advocacy by Phillips and his followers, the Department of Buildings has served Rockefeller with a violation on this issue, but they remain determined to skirt the law when they can. A sign barring the public from the lower plaza that is used on weekends sits nearby. And just two days earlier, security on the same property attempted to remove Phillips for filming on the property, though he was not breaking any of the posted rules about the plaza’s use.

In fact, as we walk from one plaza to another, I remark that Phillips seems scrupulous about following the rules of these plazas. “That’s my whole leverage,” he grins.” That’s my whole thing, is [that] I’m going to document that I’m being completely a normal guy.” The message of all his videos and advocacy is one of following the rules, and in the comments, he often pushes back when his followers urge some kind of civil disobedience. The ethos of his Instagram account and all his interactions with building personnel seems to be that the public should be respectful of these public spaces by observing the rules, and that the owners should do the same. “The issue is when they start to put their own rules into effect” and refuse to abide by their own agreements with the public, he says.

Since Phillips began making these videos, security follows him around when he is in these spaces. The evening of my visit, as we sit in the sunken plaza, a security guard watches us carefully and keeps talking into his phone. Just two days earlier, at the same spot, Phillips was removed by security.

Walking north, Phillips shows me another POPS, this one at 31 West Fifty-Second Street where, until he made videos about it, the handicapped access ramp was blocked off. It’s open, for now. Another offending restaurant on the same property has reduced its outdoor table intrusion to just one, which Phillips thinks is acceptable even if it might technically be out of line. “It’s a give-and-take,” he says, “because obviously nothing is ever perfect,” pointing out that it might be hard for an owner to completely forbid a tenant to use outside space that they’d assumed was part of the deal when they rented the space.

Phillips is not someone who has a hard time seeing the viewpoint of others, especially those in the same industry as him. “As a security guy, I work with a lot of these types of guys,” he says. “They kind of get the ego thing when they work in a building like this.” But they are not actually enforcing the law. Rather, they are enforcing the desires of a corporation uninterested in holding up their end of the bargain to the public.

Phillips says building owners are getting more fines and being issued more violations in response to his complaints. Phillips’s advocacy has engaged city officials, including the Buildings Commissioner Ahmed Tigani, who was appointed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani in January and has met with Phillips and toured the offending sites. Phillips calls Tigani “a great, great asset.” Phillips would like to see the city strengthen enforcement and streamline the process for responding to complaints; at present, it’s hampered by the fact that multiple agencies are involved (exactly the kind of problem Mamdani’s Commission on Government Efficiency [COGE] has been trying to fix). He’d also like to see city council legislation to increase the fines on repeat offenders.

div.p: Phillips also holds dance parties, concerts, and most recently, a well-attended Halloween flash dance party and costume contest in the POPS, spreading the word about the violations but also reclaiming these public spaces for public joy. For the Halloween party, Phillips himself showed up in full king regalia, including a crown and scepter — the Lord of Bench, crowned as such.

While the response to his project is satisfying so far, Phillips would like to see the real estate industry comply more fully, and he thinks Mayor Mamdani’s attention on the issue would help significantly. “This is the one issue I cannot believe he has not said a word on since the moment it started,” Phillips says, noting with some annoyance that many content creators “with far less following, with far less reach” have been in conversation with the mayor. “I’m not one of the crazy guys out here!” says Phillips. “We need his voice on this.”

Phillips’s project — fighting for public control of space against real estate oligarchs who want to take it away — seems closely aligned with Mamdani’s own. Both have been fighting for the working class to quite literally have a place in the city: a bench, an apartment, a park, a soccer field, a night at the opera. Both insist that New York is for everybody.

Phillips, for his part, does not frame his crusade in ideological terms. “This is an issue that transcends everything,” he says. “Doesn’t matter if you’re left, right, green. Everybody’s gonna sit on a bench.”

entry.summary: Many Manhattan real estate developers have a legal obligation to keep space outside their high-rise buildings open to all — yet refuse. We spoke to Lord of Bench, an activist who is taking them on to reclaim public space for the public.

entry.title: Rabid Anti-Communism Still Shapes the Politics of California

div.p: Donald Trump’s political vocabulary is not especially original. When he calls Democrats “radical left,” “Marxists,” or “hardcore godless communists,” he recycles one of the oldest weapons in American political life: the charge that political opponents are not merely wrong but fundamentally un-American because of their alleged leftist ideology.

In his rambling social media posts and ham-fisted rants, Trump uses anti-communism as a blunt political instrument. He labels proposals for expanded health care, rent control, stronger unions, and higher taxes on the wealthy as evidence of some sort of communist conspiracy. Obviously, this is not analytical precision but brutish intimidation.

California, home of coastal elites who pride themselves on leading a progressive bastion of resistance to MAGA, should not dismiss this rhetoric as something imported from the reactionary red states of flyover country. Anti-communism has deep roots in the Golden State’s political history. In California, the legal and cultural architecture of the Cold War survives today.

The irony is as beautiful as a Malibu sunset. Trump and other right-wing ideologues routinely describe California as a “communist” state, an absurd insult to direct at one of the most heavily capitalist jurisdictions on Earth.

California is home to Silicon Valley, Hollywood, immense agricultural corporations, vast real estate fortunes, and some of the most concentrated private wealth in the United States if not the world. Calling California “communist” is not political analysis; it is a silly denunciation ritual. But it is a ritual with a history behind it.

In the late 1940s and early 1950s, California was a laboratory for Cold War repression. With the 1950 Levering Act, the state legislature required public employees to take a loyalty oath. The law reflected a climate where politicians claimed Communist Party members were an internal enemy seeking to infiltrate public institutions such as schools and universities.

University of California professors who refused to sign the oath lost their positions. As a graduate student teaching assistant at the University of California, Santa Cruz, in 1990, I was required to sign an iteration of the oath in my onboarding paperwork.

Californian anti-communism produced the Cold War’s most consequential conservative presidents. Richard Nixon began his career as a California congressman by pursuing Alger Hiss through the House Un-American Activities Committee (HUAC). This red-baiting made him a nationally recognized figure.

A middling Hollywood actor who had been elected as president of the Screen Actors Guild in 1947, Ronald Reagan willingly collaborated with HUAC. In the 1950s, he starred on a weekly television show called “General Electric Theater.” As well as introducing each episode, Reagan traveled across the country to tour GE plants and deliver free-market, anti-communist speeches.

He then starred in 1962’s “The Truth About Communism,” a propaganda film whose IMDb page includes a memorable line: “Top Cast: Adolf Hitler — Aleksandr Kerensky — Ronald Reagan.” After he retired from acting, Reagan entered politics by attacking the University of California, especially its Berkeley campus, as a symbol of decadence and decline.

During his 1966 gubernatorial campaign, he conflated student protests, antiwar activism, drugs, and sexual freedom with alleged communist influence. Promising to “clean up the mess at Berkeley,” he converted hostility to campus dissent into a central conservative political issue. Governor Reagan’s contempt for the Berkeley Free Speech Movement is the direct ancestor of Trump’s vilification of Columbia’s student encampment for Gaza. There is a line from Sproul Plaza to Hind Hall.

Both Reagan and Nixon understood the domestic potential of anti-communism to discredit liberal institutions, discipline the Left, and mobilize conservative voters. Their California roots led to presidencies defined by military escalation, repression, covert intervention, and the assault on New Deal and Great Society liberalism.

With the Cold War now a fading memory, California’s anti-communist laws seemed increasingly anachronistic when State Senator Alan Lowenthal introduced Senate Bill 1322 in 2008. This would have repealed provisions that allowed the dismissal of public employees for Communist Party membership and removed related Cold War language from the state codes. The bill passed both legislative chambers but then ran into a successful countermobilization by the Vietnamese American community.

Vietnamese American lobbyists and politicians campaigned against it. Activists, including lawyer Nguyễn Quốc Lân, urged Republican Governor Arnold Schwarzenegger to veto the bill, for fear that it would permit communists to teach in California schools. Schwarzenegger answered their call, invoking the experience of Californians who had fled communist regimes and arguing that the state should keep the existing laws in place.

The episode demonstrates how anti-communism survives in the Golden State. Senate Bill 1322 would hardly have legalized violent subversion or served as a pathway to revolution. It would merely have removed archaic penalties for political affiliation while preserving the state’s power to punish advocacy of its violent overthrow. But refugees from one of the most successful revolutions in world history transformed a narrow civil liberties reform into a supposed threat to public safety.

The law’s legacy remains embedded in California’s legal bureaucracy. Government Code sections 3100–3109 still require public employees to take an oath before entering state employment. Currently the oath requires employees to support and defend the US and California constitutions, disavowing violent, unlawful revolutionary organizations.

Today California employees are not required to utter the clichéd declaration, “I am not nor have I ever been a member of the Communist Party.” Explicit Cold War anti-communism has given way to a broader prohibition on organizations advocating the overthrow of the government. But the relevant provisions flow directly from laws designed specifically to target Communist affiliation, while other sections of the Government Code still refer explicitly to Communist Party membership in background checks.

Californian anti-communism also lives on in diaspora politics. After the collapse of the US-backed South Vietnamese regime in 1975, hundreds of thousands of Vietnamese refugees arrived in the Golden State. Southern California became the center of the largest Vietnamese community outside Vietnam.

Those who fled the revolution consider April 30, 1975, to have been the date of the “fall of Saigon.” The victorious Hanoi government prefers to speak of the city’s “liberation” (before it was promptly renamed Ho Chi Minh City). These new Californians refused to celebrate April 30 as the achievement of national unification. For them, “Black April” is a moment of catastrophe.

For these refugees and their descendants, the Republic of Vietnam’s yellow flag with three red stripes represents a lost homeland, family sacrifice, and displacement, but above all a mythologized resistance to communist tyranny in the name of freedom. Just as Miami’s Little Havana recalls pre–Fidel Castro Cuba with nostalgia, and West LA’s “Tehrangeles” reimagines the shah’s Iran as an era of progressive modernity, Orange County’s Little Saigon and San Jose’s Vietnamese neighborhoods invoke the alleged heroism of the Army of the Republic of Vietnam.

In these circles, discussion of endemic corruption, rigged elections, and bustling torture rooms under US client dictatorships is not welcome. These exiles silence the memory of Fulgencio Batista’s gangsterism, the brutality of Iran’s Bureau for Intelligence and for Security of the State (SAVAK), and the tiger cages of the Saigon regime.

These newly enfranchised Southeast Asian Californians made common cause with established white anti-communist Californians. In the reactionary Reagan era of the 1980s, firebrand conservative and Vietnam combat veteran Bob Dornan moved from liberal West LA to Orange County.

Behind the Orange Curtain, Dornan exploited the trauma of Westminster’s Vietnamese refugees for his political career. In the House of Representatives, while the Californian Republican was not particularly effective in pursuing a legislative agenda, he proved to be one of the most vocal cheerleaders for Reagan’s global anti-communist crusade.

As these Vietnamese émigrés passed their rabid anti-communism onto their children, the American-born generation continued to fight their lost cause. Despite his white nationalist anti-immigrant rhetoric and policies, Trump found a pool of MAGA loyalists in Little Saigon. In some of the most surreal images from January 6, 2021, Californian Vietnamese Americans marched on the US Capitol waving the South Vietnamese flag.

In California, anti-communism is a bipartisan effort. In 2024, Democratic State Assembly member Stephanie Nguyen and her Republican colleague Tri Ta took issue with Los Angeles County’s decision to declare April 30 “Jane Fonda Day” in honor of her decades of progressive activism.

Nguyen and Ta argued that celebrating the woman dubbed “Hanoi Jane” by her detractors on April 30 was deeply hurtful to the Vietnamese community, which claims a monopoly of the date for their anti-communist rituals. Right-wing veterans and their supporters, who had never forgiven the young Fonda’s 1972 peace mission to North Vietnam, supported the protest.

California anti-communism can also take on much cruder forms. At a Trump-inspired anti-communist demonstration on Huntington Beach in 2017, a group of white men chanted, “You can’t run, you can’t hide, you’re going to get a helicopter ride,” while wearing shirts that depicted bodies falling from helicopters, invoking a global history of anti-communist state terror.

While Trump’s anti-communism is opportunistic, vulgar, and intellectually empty, it is effective because it draws upon institutions and memories that long predate him. Of course, California is not and has never been communist, but it has been and remains deeply shaped by anti-communism.

entry.summary: Donald Trump likes to brand California’s Democratic establishment as a nest of “far-left communists.” This unhinged rhetoric can still find a ready audience because it resonates with a deep-rooted Californian tradition of lurid, authoritarian red-baiting.

entry.title: Public Ownership of Key Economic Sectors Is Popular

div.p: Democratic voters overwhelmingly support the public ownership and operation of several key industries. At least one of the Democratic politicians who want to win the party’s next presidential primary should take note.

A poll I recently commissioned from the Center for Strategic Politics found that a supermajority of Democratic voters support public ownership and operation of health care and the electrical grid. A slight majority supports public ownership of the nation’s railroads. And far more voters said they would support public ownership and operation of artificial intelligence than opposed it.

img.alt: Democratic voter support for public ownership by sector

div.p: Per other polling conducted back in June, Bernie Sanders’s proposal to partially nationalize AI companies is also incredibly popular across the political spectrum. Maybe it’s the number of socialists holding public office now, or maybe it’s the Trump administration’s habit of demanding stakes in private companies, but public ownership isn’t all that taboo anymore. Not if you trust the polls.

And at least in American politics, polling has been having a moment for the last few years. Political consultants and talking heads are paid handsomely to tell politicians and partisans of both parties that they really need to consult the latest polls before deciding how they’ll campaign.

Besides the inherent issues with such an approach, polling is usually a poor way to find a novel policy proposal or a topic that candidates could win a campaign by bearing down on. Asking hundreds or thousands of prospective voters a battery of questions quickly becomes quite expensive, and while the marginal cost per question isn’t especially high, most polls focus on policy areas that are already salient. Ergo, we don’t see many polls that directly ask whether voters would support nationalizing parts of the economy, aside from questions about Medicare for All. But we do know that nationalization can be very popular.

Across gender, age group, ethnicity, and political leaning, and across polls, the economy or the cost of living is by far the issue cited most frequently as deciding Americans’ votes. Even when socialization doesn’t have any real ideological appeal for voters, pitching public ownership as a cost-of-living measure has proven to be politically effective. Just look at New York.

The poll I commissioned showed that grocery stores are one of the industries Democrats are least interested in taking into public ownership, but piloting municipally owned groceries was a key platform plank of the wildly successful Zohran Mamdani mayoral campaign. It polled quite well during the campaign and, despite significant pushback, is one of the campaign promises that Mamdani is currently working to keep.

Calls for a larger public stake in or full public ownership of other industries are far more likely to be political winners: thanks to the Hugging Face hack and similar fiascos, the public is increasingly concerned about recent developments in artificial intelligence. The war with Iran and increased demand are driving up electricity prices across the United States. And private health care and health insurance are just inherently disastrous.

Right now, Democratic voters still haven’t fully lined up behind any of the major presidential hopefuls. The largest bloc across almost every poll says it will support Kamala Harris, but a half-dozen other candidates are also polling relatively well. Most notably, democratic socialist Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez usually ends up in the top tier of serious contenders.

The poll results suggest that a properly motivated political entrepreneur could benefit from the American cost-of-living crisis quite easily. Just call to nationalize the industries that Americans want to see nationalized. If, as Substacker Matthew Yglesias suggests, the politically minded “should encourage candidates to embrace popular progressive causes,” then we should encourage candidates to embrace nationalization.

Now, maybe ambitious Democrats should not call for the nationalization of restaurants, but at a minimum, the government taking a leading role in the rapidly developing AI sector and large swaths of the private health care system appears overwhelmingly popular. As a vision to rally around, it would at least help secure them the nomination.

entry.title: Harold Cruse, the Loneliest Black Radical Intellectual

div.p: Harold Wright Cruse (1916–2005), my colleague at the University of Michigan for decades, may have been the most flamboyantly paradoxical radical intellectual ever to roam our institution’s halls. An astonishing autodidact with a wealth of knowledge about cultural and political history, Cruse authored a foundational work in black studies: The Crisis of the Negro Intellectual: A Historical Analysis of the Failure of Black Leadership (1967). Now, two decades after his death, a short, pacy biography by Villanova University theologian and Africana studies scholar Vincent W. Lloyd titled Harold Cruse: Critic, Writer, Teacher captures many of Cruse’s idiosyncrasies to present a riot of contradictions.

Cruse, a high school dropout with no college degrees, was recruited to the Michigan history department one year after the publication of Crisis, which quickly became a standard classroom text, often cited alongside Frantz Fanon’s The Wretched of the Earth (1961) and The Autobiography of Malcolm X (1965). Cruse’s book was a six-hundred-page tome bursting with insight and erudition but also ornery opinions about racial integration, black nationalism, and communism, not to mention uncharitable generalizations about women, Jews, and Caribbean immigrants. These were voiced, on and off the page, with absolute certainty and self-righteousness.

His most scathing criticisms were aimed at leading African American activists and thinkers, and his style stood out for his penchant for hurling rhetorical grenades. His targets included civil rights organizations such as the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) and Martin Luther King Jr’s Southern Christian Leadership Conference, which he saw as “motivated by selfish class interests, because the main objective of the Negro middle class is a status and a social position approximating . . . the great Anglo-American middle class.” But more often, such “Cruse missiles” were launched at the very black leftists I was teaching and admired.

Richard Wright, for example, my cultural lodestar since high school, was depicted, in language redolent of far-right Judeo-Bolshevik conspiracy theories, as “so ideologically blinded by the smog of Jewish-Marxist nationalism that he was unable to see his own clearly.” Lorraine Hansberry, James Baldwin, and Paul Robeson were part of a long list under fire for naiveté and a lack of independent, sophisticated thought. Hansberry, Cruse said, was the “Joan of Arc of People’s Integration,” and Baldwin “a rather innocent and provincial intellectual.” Robeson’s 1958 autobiographical manifesto, Here I Stand, was described as “a weak, muddled, sentimental book, suffused with innocent idealism and lacking a single paragraph of original thought on Negro problems.”

Cruse’s overall literary legacy, consisting of three books and numerous essays, left an erratic track record: a baffling mix of acuity, wide reading, personal grudges, and dubious hot takes. He used Marxist terminology but was not a Marxist, for he saw the United States as a battleground of competing racial and ethnic groups more than a conflict between economic classes. He advocated black self-determination, but at the center was culture, not land, and his notion of culture was black art, theater, literature, and media, not the less elitist anthropological definition. For Cruse, Harlem was to be the center of black autonomy, even as over 90 percent of the black population lived outside Harlem with a vastly different cultural experience.

Most problematic, as the late Trinity College Professor Jerry Gafio Watts observed in Heroism and the Black Intellectual (1994), is that he “wanted to frame the issues of black intellectual life and politics along a rather simpleminded axis between black nationalism and integrationism.” It was a questionable either-or version of the old race and class debate that still roils the Left in new forms.

Cruse’s belief that black Americans should operate as an organized ethnic interest group to bargain for power failed to challenge the capitalist foundation of American society. Was there no way for a fight for cultural self-determination, racial pride, and democratic rights against a racially oppressive system to blend with class struggle, aiming at a society with economic and social justice for all? Lloyd even speculates that, until the end of his life, Cruse wrestled with the question: “What if separate but equal was not such a bad thing?”

Lloyd’s approach to Cruse is more that of a storyteller than a historian. His focus is on the portrait of a person, not on defending or disputing Cruse’s political theories. Through a narrative based on numerous interviews and some original documentation, we soon learn that there were many Harold Cruses. That’s because Lloyd makes every effort “to allow the people who knew Cruse to speak for themselves.” People’s perceptions of memorable individuals vary by age and context, and the man who ultimately emerges from Lloyd’s portrait was not to everyone’s taste.

As an authoritative spokesperson for a particular brand of African American self-determination in the 1960s and ’70s, Cruse was both adored by acolytes and despised by those with whom he differed or whom he had offended. Many, including me, admired his ambition, his ability to pose challenging questions, and his desire to promote African American intellectual thought. We liked that he didn’t pitch softballs but were flummoxed by shortcomings in his thinking — too many grandiose claims followed by superficial analysis.

Lloyd himself is less drawn by any agreement with Cruse’s stances than by what he sees as the “critical dimension” and “spirit” of Cruse’s thought. Nevertheless, for those of us who knew Cruse, all this was complicated by how to negotiate a personal relationship with an imposing figure marked by a titanic but fragile ego.

In five chapters, Lloyd offers a rather chatty survey that begins with Cruse’s working-class family background in Virginia, his hardscrabble youth with relatives in Harlem, and his military service in World War II. Then come a half-dozen years in the Communist Party USA (CPUSA) as a journalist and librarian, followed by life as a Greenwich Village bohemian with literary aspirations in theater and fiction. Cruse next shifts into black nationalist activism and social criticism with the Liberator Magazine and the Freedom Now Party. When Crisis becomes a national publishing sensation, he is hired as a visiting black studies instructor at the University of Michigan. He retires fifteen years later as a full professor, an “elder,” and something of a legend.

Lloyd’s is a kind of magpie method, with proleptic leaps from the outset, but it proves surprisingly helpful in certain areas because, previously, only uneven source material had been available for many facets of his subject’s life. Lloyd knows how to distill the essential from the inessential and never allows archival minutiae to submerge the core concern.

Moreover, Lloyd is no slouch in the revelation department. Cruse was ostentatious about name-dropping and telling tales of his army experiences in North Africa and Italy, as well as his 1960 trip to Cuba sponsored by the Fair Play for Cuba Committee. But he was mostly tight-lipped about his personal and emotional past. This left some of us wondering how dark his secrets might be.

As it turns out, most of Cruse’s closeted skeletons are the familiar human ones — a love life Lloyd can’t untangle and some problematic episodes with alcohol. On the other hand, there is the revelation from Freedom of Information Act records that Cruse “named about a dozen of his former [Communist] party associates as Communist Party members” to the FBI, even as he would later deny any such cooperation. Sometimes not all the facts in a person’s life are convenient, and often the lies we tell about the past seem necessary to live in the present. Still, this is a whopper that will leave many of his acquaintances with the taste of ashes in their mouths.

Otherwise, what Lloyd unravels is a long life with many loops, interludes, and repetitions. At times, it’s something of a detective story as he tries to figure out whether Cruse was ever legally married, whether he abandoned a son in Europe, and whether the sweep of Cruse’s career reads more like a rise and slide than a rise and fall. After a twenty-year wait and many false starts, his final book, Plural but Equal: A Critical Study of Blacks and Minorities and America’s Plural Society, appeared in 1987. Instead of a late-life powerhouse performance, it was judged to add little to his thesis that the United States was a society of competing ethnic blocs, and it has been effectively out of print for nearly four decades.

We learn about many elements of Cruse’s baroque personality — highly complex, dramatic, extravagant, and emotionally intense. With ramrod posture and a face often set in a dignified pose, he projected brooding bitterness and the aura of a man who felt personally wronged. At Michigan, he seemed to swing between episodes of immense energy and passion and periods of existential rumination, with students both benefiting and suffering. Through it all, Lloyd is remarkably nonjudgmental. He rightly seems to accept the mysteries of the shadowlands of human motivations. He has no desire to canonize a saint and recognizes that Cruse was somewhat intoxicated with his own sense of self-importance. I would also add that, intellectually, Cruse was the type who always needed to have a foil.

For me, the arc of Cruse’s life felt awe-inspiring. A true boundary crosser, he was catapulted from plebeian marginality to superstar fame, mainly through ulcer-producing hard work and an authentic, self-authored identity that I associated with my own Marxist-existentialist aspirations. Lloyd, however, shows that certain fortuitous friendships (a Jewish couple with publishing connections) and political coincidences (a black student revolt at the University of Michigan) also helped his rise.

Yet despite our fundamentally different political orientations, some of us on the Left were attracted to Cruse’s intellectual stridency, not to mention the exciting charge of his transgressive opinions. Attacking orthodoxies and stomping on taboos — what’s not to like? After all, I, too, was working on a book-length call to arms for a new approach based on a critical reassessment of the Left’s past record on culture and intellectuals. That my focus was on Jews, and that I was Jewish, never seemed to be a problem for him, despite his oft-expressed wariness of Jewish Marxist intellectuals.

Moreover, having read much C. L. R. James and George Breitman’s 1967 book, The Last Year of Malcolm X, I was open to the idea of an independent black liberation movement as a vanguard catalyst that did not need to subordinate itself to a conservatized white working class. To be sure, I was hardly an expert on the chameleon ideology of nationalism, but I sympathized with anti-colonialism and opposed expansionist and chauvinistic nationalism. One could be suspicious of any claims of nationalist belonging and yet reject the facile stereotype of all varieties of nationalism as equally essentialist and ethnocentric.

I felt most politically at odds with Cruse on the centrality of intellectuals, ultimate economic goals, and the black movement’s relationship to the white working class. As for his treatment of the CPUSA, my own research had convinced me that one can be correct about its Stalinist politics but wrong about almost everything else. Cruse had grossly misrepresented both the sincerity and the impact of the CPUSA members’ commitment to anti-racism, and in this regard Crisis read too much like a pulpy novel of revenge.

Lloyd’s interview findings match my own experiences with Cruse. I first met him at events sponsored by Michigan’s Center for Afroamerican and African Studies in 1975, just after his brief term as an early director. After several discussions about his CPUSA experiences, he gave me an autographed copy of a long and remarkable course description for “Marxism and the Negro Question,” a class he took at the CPUSA’s Jefferson School in the late 1940s. Then, in the fall of 1979, he requested a favor: Would I take over some reviewing assignments he had promised the socialist newspaper In These Times? This would start with James Baldwin’s new novel Just Above My Head (1979), which he found “unreadable.” As an untenured nobody, I was quite flattered, and this review led to eight more, on writers such as Hansberry, W. E. B. Du Bois, and my fellow English department member Gayl Jones.

For the next fifteen years, during which time he officially retired in 1984, we continued our association, although I mainly queried him for information on his CPUSA comrades with little reciprocal curiosity. Then, in the spring of 1992, I invited the emeritus Cruse to address two sessions of a seminar I had organized on the cultural left in the 1950s; the plan was to juxtapose chapters of Crisis against one of Cruse’s objects of criticism — the novel Youngblood (1954) by the pro-Communist leader of the Harlem Writers Guild, John Oliver Killens. Cruse seemed pleased, and I opened the first class with a fulsome introduction, including a biographical sketch with highlights of his career that I thought he might have been too modest to mention himself. To my surprise, the discussion that ensued around Killens was stilted and relatively unproductive.

When I met with Cruse afterward, he gave me a sharp dressing-down; nothing I had said was inaccurate or disrespectful, but he had wanted to represent himself, not have me do it for him. This was followed by a letter explaining that he would not return to the seminar, but for a different reason: “To be honest, I never finished reading Youngblood after it was published. For me, the novel possessed no literary merit.” Sheesh, I thought, why didn’t he say that in the first place?

Lloyd’s biography, however, discloses a history of similar behavior — walking offstage, hanging up mid-conversation, and precipitously dumping a graduate student — and I likely got off easy. Just four months later, we were back in dialogue. He wanted to learn what I had heard about Van Gosse’s book in progress about the Fair Play for Cuba Committee, although he did manage to stick in an admonishment about my allegedly teaching Youngblood as a “masterpiece.”

The point is that Cruse had an unsleeping vigilance for any possible slight, which was a significant element in his alienation from the CPUSA. As Lloyd reveals, Hansberry and others he saw as an insider group under CPUSA control rebuffed his aspirations to write for the theater in the 1950s. And as Lloyd convincingly argues, “Cruse’s ideas . . . grew out of Cruse’s life.” But too much of it was a synthetic certainty about the motives and achievements of a bricolage of black communist cultural dupes: “White intellectuals are unoriginal, imitative, and puerile, and black intellectuals are brainwashed by the whites.”

Throughout his writing, he hammers this theme like Vulcan, rolling over it relentlessly from new angles — casting would-be African American radical intellectuals as betrayed by West Indians, manipulated by Jews, and undermined by black women. No wonder one of Cruse’s most impressive legacies has been highly sophisticated, well-researched refutations, starting with the concluding section of Winston James’s Holding Aloft the Banner of Ethiopia: Caribbean Radicalism in Early Twentieth Century America (1999).

The longer one ponders Cruse, the more enigmatic his beguiling strangeness becomes. Yes, he was always available for discussion and consultation, yet this seemed tethered to a thirst for adulation. His inner life is not my story to tell, and he had a perpetually inscrutable aura. I quickly saw I would never be the yin to his yang — far from it. It was hard not to sense that his personality contained many combustible elements that, mixed at high velocity, might explode. I, and probably many others, handled him with kid gloves. But did I ever actually see him for who he was?

Perhaps the crucial insight comes from a private letter to his mother that Lloyd quotes early in his biography: “I have grown up mostly alone. I have always been forced to be reliant on no one but myself.” Simone de Beauvoir, among others, has written about the deep emotional isolation that comes from complete self-reliance, but surely the price is tenfold for a working-class African American like Cruse aspiring to literary fame. His may superficially resemble the familiar radical individualism of those of us who reject what we believe are prepackaged identities handed down by others. But for Cruse, it was a new and self-owned identity agonizingly forged in the crucible of a white-racist and class-divided society.

Cruse was no doubt as guilty as the rest of us at times in acquiescing to opportunistic acts of self-preservation. At Michigan, although he taught pioneering and successful classes, he was no ally in the activist campaigns against South African apartheid and US intervention in Latin America. He sneered at most campus activism. If he was not the leading man, he wasn’t going to play a supporting role.

Moreover, his anti-communism fed Cold War myths, and many of his attitudes about gender were retrograde even by the standards of his generation. Although commonly regarded as a black cultural nationalist, he was hypercritical of the movement’s leaders and a splinter in its toe as well. Nevertheless, he is hardly alone among his generation in being disoriented by the Stalinist experience, and I see his obsessive writing as testimony to an undying struggle to define his own life and create his own meaning. The loneliness of the black radical intellectual was perhaps the most direct price he paid for this autonomy.

entry.title: Only Israel’s Palestinians Vote Against Genocide

div.p: It was heralded by many as “the most consequential election in Israeli history,” and by rights it should have been. Under Benjamin Netanyahu’s outgoing far-right government, Israel plunged into a severe constitutional crisis, suffered the worst military setback in its history, carried out a genocide in Gaza and two failed wars in Iran, and become the most hated country in the world.

And yet, as Haaretz editor Aluf Benn noted in his postmortem, Israeli Jewish voters proved themselves imperturbable. Support for aggression throughout the region remains nearly universal among Jewish voters, who have once again sorted themselves again into pro- and anti-Netanyahu blocs on a basis that, while reflecting real class divisions, is expressed in familiar culture-war terms, producing yet another frustrating stalemate.
There is, however, one dramatic exception to this uncanny stasis: Israel’s Palestinian minority, which responded to unprecedented levels of racist incitement with the highest turnout on record.

Of over eight hundred thousand votes cast by Palestinian citizens, 37 percent went to the Islamist United Arab List (UAL, also known as Ra’am), and 51 percent to the Joint List, which unites communists, left-liberals and independents. As a result, nineteen out of 120 seats in the Knesset, which are allocated proportionally, have gone to Israel’s only two non-Zionist parties, each of which also has one Jewish representative. (Support for these parties among Jews is numerically insignificant, though hundreds of Jewish academics signed a petition in support of the Joint List.)

In stark contrast to the violence and malaise that have gripped Israel’s Palestinian community following the rise of state-tolerated organized crime, the contest between the two parties was peaceful and restrained. This is all the more remarkable given the clear ideological divide between them.

The Joint List couples the demand for civic equality for Palestinian citizens with a clear rejection of Israel’s annihilationist policy in Gaza and its ethnic cleansing in the West Bank. Meanwhile, the UAL — a prominent member of the original Joint List — has turned to a sectoral strategy modeled on that of Israel’s ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties. Following his 2021 split from the Joint List, UAL leader Mansour Abbas courted Netanyahu and then served as a junior partner in the government that briefly ousted him in 2021–22.

This time around, the anti-Netanyahu bloc has drawn the bar for cooperation at a level meant to exclude even the UAL. Its leader du jour, Lieutenant General Gadi Eisenkot, clarified that any party seeking to join him in government would have to declare Hamas — which still is hanging onto power in Gaza — a “terrorist organization which must be annihilated.”

As Israel Defense Forces chief of staff, Eisenkot elaborated the infamous “Dahiya doctrine,” which recommends mass killing of civilians in areas dominated by hostile forces. In the current context, his shibboleth cannot be read as anything but a demand for active consent to ongoing genocide.

The hostility of the Zionist opposition to any form of solidarity with Gaza was driven home when all its parties, including the liberal Democrats, backed an election board decision to bar Joint List candidate Sami Abu-Shehadeh from running on the basis of a vaguely celebratory article written on October 7 and subsequently repudiated. (Genocidal expressions by right-wing candidates, it goes without saying, were not censured in the same way.)

Given the depth of the racist rejectionism Palestinian citizens have suffered from both Zionist blocs and the eager complicity of both in colonial violence, a turn to abstention would not be unexpected. But Israel’s Palestinian citizens do not have the luxury of ignoring the differences between these blocs, small as they may be.

Thus, Netanyahu’s finance minister and West Bank “viceroy” Bezalel Smotrich has empowered settler militias to carry out a campaign of ethnic cleansing that might be halted, if not reversed, under an Eisenkot administration. His ghoulish national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, has made a fetish out of torturing and executing Palestinian prisoners.

High Palestinian turnout has severely weakened extreme-right parties led by the two and prevented two others from crossing the representation threshold, depriving Netanyahu’s coalition of its majority. Voters are justified in hoping a new government will dial back its ferocity on both fronts as well as tackling organized crime more seriously. For Palestinians, these are questions of life and death, if not of imminent decolonization.

Under these complex circumstances, voters have rewarded the Joint List for striking a balance between principle and pragmatism. Sociologist Maha Sabbah-Karkabi, who will be joining the Knesset as a Joint List representative, stressed the importance of Palestinians’ show of collective power. “By fully utilizing their electoral potential,” she told me, they “have repositioned themselves at the center of Israel’s political landscape.”

However, Sabbah-Karkabi added, the Joint List now confronts a “climate of delegitimization of Arab political participation coming from different parts of the political spectrum,” rendering the question of influencing government policy “much more complicated.”

Delegitimization has come swiftly from Netanyahu’s propaganda organs, which quickly coined the felicitous oxymoron “ballot box terrorism” while weakly claiming Qatari interference on the Joint List’s behalf. (Netanyahu’s advisers, of course, are the ones who have worked for Qatar.) But while Eisenkot and most of his allies obstinately continue to refuse any alliance with Palestinian parties, the Democrats are finally beginning to peel away from this boneheaded consensus.

For the Joint List, the situation presents opportunities as well as risks. Sabbah-Karkabi and Amjad Shbita, general secretary of the Democratic Front for Peace and Equality (the largest of the Joint List’s components), agree that seeing Netanyahu and his far-right government replaced is an urgent priority. Unlike the UAL’s deputies, however, they are also committed to Palestinian national solidarity across borders. The electorate has endorsed this commitment in no uncertain terms.

The ball is now in the court of Eisenkot’s anti-Netanyahu bloc. To avoid a return election, he will have to break one of two campaign promises: not to enter a coalition with Netanyahu, and to avoid relying on “Arab votes.” If he reneges on the former vow — perhaps under cover of a new war with Iran, conveniently started by Donald Trump and Netanyahu in the coming weeks — he will gift the latter with a renewed sheen of invincibility and the international legitimacy he has done so much to lose.

To end Netanyahu’s rule, Eisenkot would have to break the racist taboo on negotiation with the Palestinian public’s representatives. Though it will not join an Eisenkot government, Shbita told me, the Joint List would be willing to provide it with a parliamentary safety net, preventing Netanyahu from getting another shot at power by bringing the government down with a vote of no confidence.

Even if Eisenkot lacks the courage to negotiate such an agreement, Shbita added, “we would consider enabling a minority government by not voting it down until Netanyahu’s departure from the political scene becomes a certainty.”

Following the “most consequential election in its history,” the political scene in Israel continues to look unbearably bleak. Progressives elsewhere have no reason to let up the pressure for broad sanctions and a total arms embargo. Nevertheless, they can take inspiration from the many Palestinian (and a few Jewish) citizens of Israel, who by voting for the Joint List have expressed their steadfastness — sumoud — in the struggle for democracy, justice, and peace.

entry.title: The Iran War Might Soon Get Catastrophically Worse

div.p: Between all the action around next week’s midterms and Donald Trump’s meddling in Brazilian politics, it’s easy to forget there’s a war going on. But sure enough, Trump’s war on Iran is still humming in the background, and every indication is that it could flare up in a terrible new way very soon.

According to multiple reports, Trump has been planning a renewed attack on Iran that is likely to be launched after the midterms, though according to the Wall Street Journal, the president had not yet firmly decided whether he’ll go through with it. The renewed attack, the Journal reports, would be a “short, intense war” that would hit Iranian infrastructure, its munition arsenal, and its nuclear sites, or at least that’s what sources have told the US press. Sen. Chris Murphy, who has been briefed on some of the attack plans, has called them “insane” and said they would lead to “the likely destruction of our commitment to the rule of law,” which suggests something potentially broader and even more extreme.

Funnily enough, a month before any of this reporting was published, Quincy Institute Executive Vice President Trita Parsi had predicted to me that Trump was likely to do this, as a way of trying to end the war on his terms. “Trump has come to a space in his mind in which he believes that he has already tried everything. He’s tried diplomacy. He’s tried sanctions. He’s tried limited war,” Parsi said in mid-September.

“The only thing he hasn’t tried is all of those different military threats he issued early on, but never exercised: taking out the desalination plants, taking out Iran’s energy infrastructure, taking one of the islands in the Persian Gulf. I think after the midterms, that is what he’s going to try.”

Trump has, not surprisingly, been egged on in this by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who in the lead-up to the Israeli election this week repeatedly vowed to restart the war against Iran and “overthrow” the remnants of the regime there. But according to the Israeli press, Netanyahu went beyond merely pushing for war: he actively looked to start one with a planned attack on Iran that he was ultimately talked out of. As Netanyahu openly said this week on Twitter/X, he and Israel had a narrow “window of time” to act — specifically, “another two years of Trump to finish the work in Iran.”

Netanyahu’s obvious attempts to spark renewed war with Iran briefly became an election issue in Israel, when one of his opponents announced he had requested a treason investigation into the prime minister over his “pressuring the heads of the security establishment to take steps that could create a miscalculation vis-à-vis Iran,” and trying to “drag the state of Israel into war on the eve of elections.” Netanyahu has a history, especially over the past three years, of using war as a means of keeping himself in power, and it’s not hard to see how a war with Iran — particularly one he could sell as being started by Tehran — could give him a popularity boost.

Netanyahu’s efforts to do this may not have worked out for the moment, but the currently deadlocked Israeli election result, combined with Trump’s preexisting plans to restart the war as soon as a week from now, could give him another shot at it. If Netanyahu’s opposition remains unable to form a government, he will stay on as caretaker prime minister until the next election, by which point a US war with Iran may well have provided a shot in the arm to his far-right coalition.

But however “insane” and brutal this latest US bombing campaign turns out to be, it’s unlikely to give Trump what he wants: for Tehran to soften its demands and take a deal that’s worse for them and better for him.

Trump’s actions — including his repeated violation of agreements and diplomatic protocols, and the sneak attack that killed scores of Iranian officials at the start of the war — have thoroughly delegitimized Iran’s moderates and placed the country firmly in the hands of hard-liners who oppose negotiations, and some of whom do things like move to impeach the country’s more pro-diplomacy foreign minister.

These hard-liners believe that any deal Iran strikes with Washington is pointless, because Trump or his successor will just rip it up later regardless. The hard-liners are convinced the only way to ensure both the state’s and the country’s survival is to inflict such costs on the United States and its political leadership that they’ll leave their country alone. They are also, ironically, now looking seriously at actually pursuing a nuclear weapon — a pursuit Iran’s previous supreme leader had, it turns out, been the main roadblock to, until Trump dropped a bomb on his house in February and killed him.

Trump still reportedly hopes that using military force will this time stop Iran from making a bomb. But that idea is likely to run into the same problem as before: namely, that Iran’s buried nuclear sites are basically unreachable, even by the largest bombs the United States can drop on them, so he would need to launch a risky ground operation to extract the enriched material that still wouldn’t be guaranteed of success. Look at how costly the vastly less complicated effort to recover a single pilot in April proved, and you start to get a sense of the difficulty with this idea.

Meanwhile, Iran’s new hard-line leadership is willing to absorb (or more accurately, willing to let the Iranian people take) a tremendous amount of pain to achieve this, as they have demonstrated. Years of preexisting suffering under US sanctions and a rally-’round-the-flag effect that has seen anti-government dissent evaporate means life in Iran is persisting in the face of widespread shortages, nearly 90 percent inflation, and at least $270 billion worth of destroyed infrastructure.

So what would a “short, intense war” on Iran actually do, then? Besides the human toll on ordinary Iranians just trying to live their lives, it would likely mean even worse blowback on everyone else, the United States included.

Like Trump, Iran’s leaders have military cards they haven’t played yet, and they are openly threatening much worse retaliation this time if they’re attacked again. Iranian officials have threatened to make the war “longer and in a wider geographical area,” and to inflict a “devastating impact” on energy markets, aiming to shove the world into outright recession and create a large-scale refugee crisis. Surrounding oil facilities, ports, pipelines, refineries, power grids, and even desalination plants have been mentioned as targets.

This would be devastating for — and in the case of power grids and desalination plants, existentially threatening to — life in the Gulf states, whose economies have already been battered by the war. This is why a host of Iran’s neighbors, including Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey, have been desperately holding talks with Tehran to try to stop what might be the most devastating round of an already regionally destructive war, so far with no tangible results.

But it’s not just Iran’s neighbors who will bear the brunt of this. Iran’s leaders specifically named as targets the undersea cables that carry internet traffic and the trillions of dollars of infrastructure in the region that the US artificial intelligence industry relies on, including data centers. That industry, which Trump is heavily relying on to prop up the US economy, is already showing serious signs of strain in the face of mounting financial losses and growing investor skepticism. Major damage to critical infrastructure and resulting market disruption risks adding further strain on an industry that many already fear is a bubble waiting to pop. In its recent initial public offering prospectus, AI firm Anthropic specifically mentioned the fact that “armed conflict” could damage or destroy data centers and other infrastructure as one of its risk factors, a warning that other industry players have made.

More ominously, a senior Iranian security official has also named “US political targets” as potentially fair game. Recall, too, that Iran is widely believed to be the culprit behind months of cyberattacks on a variety of US infrastructure, including water systems. If either of these is part of Iran’s next retaliatory move, it would not only cause intense chaos and suffering for the US public but potentially trigger a dangerous escalation spiral.
Vice President J. D. Vance has reportedly now reached out to Iran’s hard-line top security chief to resuscitate peace talks. Given everything laid out above, this would be wise.

The trouble is that the two parties here remain a canyon apart. Iranian leadership views it as effectively suicide to budge from the terms they agreed to earlier this year, while Trump has been led to view those terms as a personal humiliation, so he keeps trying and failing to bomb or blockade his way to a more favorable deal after the fact. There is also the wild card of Netanyahu, who has already more than once tried to single-handedly torpedo a Trump-Iran deal by bombing Lebanon and violating one of Iran’s core demands.

The White House now is certain that Iran is on the brink of capitulation, and all it will take is one more push to get it there. In reality, Trump is dealing with an Iran that is more dangerous and less likely to capitulate than ever: not because it has a nuke, but because years of Trump’s own foolish policy choices have turned it into an adversary that sees itself as having nothing to lose — and is acting like it, which is why Iranian leaders are effetively threatening that if they go down, they will take the entire region as well as the global economy with them.

Trump and the people around him are looking at next week’s midterms as the moment they will be unshackled from political constraints, freeing them to take the reckless, escalatory measures they were reluctant to take before for fear of voter backlash. If they were smart, they would treat it as freeing them instead to take the deal they had already agreed to, and to just swallow the inevitable political point-scoring and cries of “capitulation” that are, sadly, now just standard whenever any president tries to end a war.

But it is clear that there is a dearth of voices around the president that are inclined to tell him this. It is increasingly likely that Trump soon takes a step that will prove even more terrible for the country, for his political party, and his own legacy.

entry.title: Preparing for MAGA’s Worst on Election Day

div.p: Imagine this: Election Day comes and goes. Democrats turn out big and flip a few seats, some by close margins. Forces opposing the increasingly authoritarian drift of the United States breathe a sigh of relief.

Before the results are even called, however, Donald Trump declares in a wave of Truth Social posts that Democrats have cheated, the results are fraudulent, and those responsible will be prosecuted and persecuted. By the next day, the claims have spread to congressional Republicans, who vow to seek justice — and, in some cases, vengeance — for the supposed voter fraud.

Protesters take to the streets in several cities, demanding that all votes be counted. They call on their representatives to stand behind voters’ democratic wishes. The protests spread, and on November 6, Trump claims that protesters in several cities have gotten out of hand and broken windows. He then declares that Iran has engaged in cyber election interference, thereby invalidating the results of the vote. Trump announces he will send in the National Guard and invoke the Insurrection Act to defend the country against these incursions.

Is this scenario likely? It’s hard to say. The midterms are shaping up to be a rout of the Republicans, with Trump and his party facing nearly unprecedented unfavorability and losses so great that even his normal bluster and lies about stolen elections won’t be able to hold his diminishing base. In Brazil this week, Flávio Bolsonaro floated a Trumpian trial balloon by claiming the presidential election was stolen by the Workers’ Party’s Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, but the nearly 4.5-million-vote margin that Lula won by made such mendacity absurd, and Bolsonaro has since fled the country for Miami.

But given the antidemocratic drift of the United States over the past decade and since Trump’s second election in particular, this scenario is far from impossible. Indeed, parts of it, like Trump’s denial of the election results, seem all but assured. And as the president feels his mandate in the country (and perhaps his own mental health) slipping away, who knows what a newly desperate Trump will do.

He would not be alone in taking such steps. Scholars who study authoritarianism call them an “authoritarian playbook”: a set of similar steps leaders like Flávio Bolsonaro’s former president father Jair, former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán in Hungary, and Recep Tayyip Erdoğan in Turkey have taken to consolidate power. It includes going after critics through investigations and harassment, installing loyalists, expanding federal powers, crushing dissent, and deploying military forces on their own citizens.

The Trump administration has been moving through the playbook at record speed, from firing federal workers to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) shootings to the attacks on Rep. Ilhan Omar. Unions, community and faith organizations, immigrant rights groups, and lawyers have resisted and slowed the attacks, but that hasn’t stopped Trump. His administration has already taken steps to undermine the 2026 midterm elections, attempting to restrict mail ballots, purge voter rolls, and mess with ballots in Alaska. They plan to send ICE to the polls. And Rep. Tim Burchett (R-TN) has announced plans to try to block the seating of democratic socialist Darializa Avila Chevalier, the likely next House member from New York’s Thirteenth District, while MAGA is building the legal case to do exactly that.

The task for socialists is not to vote and defend elections in order to return to the status quo, but to defend basic democratic norms while putting forth a vision of a different future. Lots of people care about elections and will be looking for answers if things go wrong. Socialists cannot sit on the sidelines. We need to challenge racist gerrymandering and minoritarian institutions like the Supreme Court and Senate to weaken the stranglehold of the authoritarian right on the federal government in order to have the opportunity to advance reforms that can establish new social and economic rights. Attacks on elections are tied to attacks on our rights to organize and protest, our rights to independent media, and our rights to engage in the democratic institutions we fought hard to create.

And for a growing share of the socialist movement, contesting for governing power via elections is a key part of the strategy. The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) are set to send seven, and potentially as many as ten, members to Congress; their strategy depends on fair elections that get those members seated so they can build a bloc that pushes for transformative demands.

We can’t develop a full plan ahead of time, but we can develop our planning skills under crisis. National organizations and some unions have already been training people on potential election scenarios through versions of “tabletop exercises” where organizers role-play different scenarios and develop strategy and tactics together. The more we practice, the easier it might be to respond when a crisis hits.

One possible scenario to come out of next week’s election is a state of confusion, where vote counting is challenged or stopped in a state or two, and courts are going back and forth about what to do. This would be similar to what happened in 2000, when the initial presidential vote count in Florida showed George W. Bush beating Al Gore by only 1,784 votes. Gore called for a recount in some counties, including Miami-Dade. Republican operatives moved quickly to send in staffers to protest outside the recount, eventually rushing the doors and attacking people, resulting in the recount being called off. After more back-and-forth, the case went to the Supreme Court, which called for an end to the recount.

Rather than protesting, Democratic Party leaders, including Gore (who would have won in a full recount), accepted the loss. This time around, we need to be ready to respond to ballot and legal confusion without waiting for courts to decide.

If we have another Florida-type scenario, such as Republican operatives refusing to count all the ballots in Texas, then socialists and all our allies need to be ready to fight back. People around the country, whether in blue, red, or purple states, can fill the streets and pressure their representatives, especially Democrats, to demand that every vote is counted. Legal observers and traditional election groups are working to protect voter registration, ensure access to polls, and prepare legal challenges. No Kings will be ready to call for mass peaceful marches. May Day Strong is preparing for economic disruption if needed, examining how people can undermine the corporate pillars that are supporting Trump’s authoritarianism.

There are billionaires and corporations directly profiting from surveillance, ICE contracts, war, and deregulation: they have a material interest in Trump’s success. Some billionaires, such as Peter Thiel and Elon Musk, go beyond that and have an ideological commitment to authoritarianism of various forms. Using the full toolbox of boycotts, sit-ins, slowdowns, walkouts, and strikes, how can we best target the billionaires and corporations who are enabling and profiting from authoritarianism, like Amazon and Jeff Bezos, and how can we encourage others, like Jamie Dimon at JPMorgan Chase and Delta Air Lines, to defect from the authoritarian coalition by making it too costly to stay?

Working in a broad front, a wide range of political actors who may oppose Trump’s antidemocratic measures but disagree with us on most everything else, to defeat authoritarianism can be simple on the one hand, because there is one unifying task: build the biggest “we” possible to defeat MAGA. But broad front politics get complicated fast. It means working with mainstream Democrats who often seem more intent on destroying DSA than MAGA. It might mean working with anti-Trump Republicans, who see socialists as the second-biggest threat after authoritarians. And it requires being in alignment with a whole host of organizations that can be annoying or disruptive or way too verbose.

Working in a broad front requires patience, education, and skill. But it also opens up the space to work with millions of people who are newly engaged by the real threat MAGA poses to their lives or jobs.

As Ash-Lee Henderson reminds us, 89 million people didn’t vote in 2024. People are angry about the cost of living, and many want and need big changes, from Medicare for All to reliable transit to an end to war. The Democratic Party has made little to no effort to acknowledge these 89 million and their frustrations, leaving the job to socialists or right-wing extremists.

To stay anchored in a broad front, socialists need nested strategies: a short-term strategy to block the authoritarian right and a longer-term strategy to build the Left. We can do that by emphasizing the capacities we need to build no matter the task: democratic participation, mass training and education on the issues that matter, door-knocking and talking with coworkers, organizing unions and mapping workplaces. We’ll need these skills to defend the midterm results; if we can do them well, we’ll connect with thousands of new people joining the fight — and be in stronger shape to shift from defense to offense.

Since the start of the second Trump administration, many unions, DSA chapters, and community organizations have had to develop the ability for rapid response against the federal government’s attacks on our neighbors. We have called protests against federal workforce union busting, developed mutual aid networks to support immigrants, and trained ourselves in direct action.

By getting more organized at a block-by-block level, we can prepare for the possibility of Republicans seriously contesting the results of our elections and make sure we are ready to organize more workers who know that we need a real voice not just in our workplaces but in our political system too. Building these muscles puts us in better shape for actions in 2028, including influencing the presidential primaries and election, and a potential May 1, 2028, national strike.

Our tasks: Vote. Get trained on noncooperation and strike readiness. Sign a pledge to defend the elections through targeted actions on corporations and elected officials. If things get messy, be ready to help coworkers and neighbors make sense of the moment and invite them into the organizations that are fighting for a better world.

entry.title: Dolores Huerta Taught a Generation How to Organize

div.p: When I came back from a solidarity work brigade in Cuba in the 1970s, I landed in New York City with no place to sleep. I called Lori Huerta, a friend from California, and daughter of Dolores Huerta (1930–2026), cofounder of the United Farm Workers (UFW). Not only did I get space on the floor of the NYC grape boycott headquarters, but Dolores and her partner, Richard, César Chávez’s brother, took us out to eat. Over pizza I enthused about the island. I had stars in my eyes, for both Cuba and Dolores, and still do. I went to work for the UFW as an organizer a few months later.

img.alt: Dolores Huerta, with Danny Glover and others, demonstrating against the Iraq War.

figure.figcaption: At the beginning of the Iraq War, Huerta marches with actor Danny Glover and an enormous crowd demanding that the troops be brought home. (Courtesy David Bacon)

div.p: Over the years, long after I had left the UFW and worked for other unions and then as a photojournalist, I would see Dolores again and again. Going to Watsonville to cover the organizing drives of strawberry workers or to Salinas for the strikes in the vegetable fields, I knew she’d be there. It was a profound experience to watch her in union contract negotiations — this diminutive woman facing off against the beefy growers across the table — and see the sense of power it gave workers. For Dolores and Eliseo Medina, another of my teachers, being a good organizer was the bottom line — doing what the workers needed.

María Elena Durazo, who came from a farmworker family to head the Los Angeles Labor Federation and now sits in the legislature, remembered, “In that world of rural California, it was the grape strike and the boycotts that taught us that the only way to end poverty and injustice was to organize together. It was the United Farm Workers who taught us that, and Dolores was the best teacher among many good ones.”

Returning from Iraq, where I photographed workers after the 2003 US invasion, I took her picture in the front line of marchers against the war. When we were in Sacramento trying to stop the anti-immigrant, anti–affirmative action, anti-bilingual initiatives, she was the first to speak out.

There was often tension in the UFW about radical politics, and being called a “red” was sometimes the route out the door. Fear of saying anything that could lead to getting fired enabled César Chávez to exert such power that even otherwise aggressive and militant organizers and workers, like Dolores, didn’t challenge him, whether about sexual abuse or political purges. Abuse is a fact in other unions I’ve belonged to, and progressive leaders have stayed quiet there too. We have to confront this system of male supremacy directly, and I know she believed this.

img.alt: Dolores Huerta, among others, demonstrating for immigration reform.

figure.figcaption: At the start of the Immigrant Workers Freedom Ride in San Francisco, Huerta and hotel workers marched to demand immigrant reform. (Courtesy David Bacon)

div.p: Her relationship with the Democratic Party was complicated. She supported some movements for political independence in the 1990s while also campaigning for mainstream Democrats. As the union’s political director, she got the California legislature to pass a union recognition bill far better than the National Labor Relations Act, as well as pesticide protections and overtime that don’t even exist in other states. Randy Villegas, our hope for breaking the MAGA stranglehold on the southern San Joaquin Valley, is someone she’s had her eye on for years. You could call her a realist.

Four years ago I walked with Dolores from Poplar to Delano, California, in honor of Larry Itliong, who started the 1965 grape strike and boycott there. She was ninety-one then, and I had a hard time keeping up. She sent me a note afterward that ended, “Sí Se Puede con El Rojo Tocino.” It was a beautiful joke.

img.alt: Dolores Huerta marches with San Joaquin Valley farmworkers and activists.

figure.figcaption: Huerta marches with San Joaquin Valley farmworkers and activists, celebrating the birthday of Larry Itliong, the Filipino leader who started the 1965 grape strike. (Courtesy David Bacon)

div.p: “Sí Se Puede” are three words we all use now, but she invented this confident way of saying “Yes We Can!” “Tocino” was the nickname the union gave me in the years I worked as an organizer — it means “bacon,” my last name. And calling me “El Rojo,” or “The Red,” in this way honored my politics.
So when she called me El Rojo Tocino, I thought, “What a compliment!” I hope I live up to it.
