entry.title: Minneapolis Refused to Take Trump’s Bait. It Paid Off.

div.p: All signs point toward a resounding rebuke of Donald Trump in Tuesday’s midterm elections. Democrats have opened up a commanding lead in national polls, Trump’s popularity has sunk to historic lows, and even many of his former supporters are turning against him.

There are plenty of reasons for this collapse, from rising prices to Trump’s disastrous war with Iran. But we shouldn’t forget what was arguably the single most important turning point of his presidency: the defeat of his militarized assault on Minneapolis.

In January, Trump’s administration set out to terrorize immigrants, crush resistance, and establish the precedent that federal forces could occupy American cities against the wishes of their residents and elected officials. Instead, it encountered a mass movement whose courage and discipline forced Washington into a humiliating retreat.

The political fallout was immediate. By late January, a Reuters poll found Trump’s overall approval had fallen to 38 percent, matching its lowest point of his second term to date. His approval on immigration, previously his strongest political asset, had sunk to 39 percent. Minneapolis had helped turn Trump’s signature political strength into a liability.

In retrospect, this outcome can seem inevitable. Surely Trump’s attacks were so excessive, his agents so brutal, and the killings of Renée Good and Alex Pretti so shocking that a national backlash was bound to follow?

But nothing was predetermined. Indeed, there’s compelling evidence that Trump and his advisers had a plan with a real chance of working: provoke Minnesota into a social explosion, whose grassroots violence and property destruction would serve as a pretext for polarizing the country and escalating Trump’s crackdown on dissent and democracy nationwide.

Similar strategies have worked for authoritarian governments in other times and places. In Minneapolis, the trap failed because of the movement’s exceptionally high level of organization and nonviolent discipline.

It’s clear that ICE, under administration orders, was consciously provoking the people of Minneapolis this past winter. Thousands of heavily armed, poorly trained federal agents flooded the Twin Cities. Masked officers conducted aggressive raids, detained residents, confronted legal observers, and deployed chemical weapons against protesters. On January 7, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent shot and killed Renée Good, a thirty-seven-year-old mother. And rather than de-escalate, Washington doubled down.

On January 13, Trump warned Minnesota that a “DAY OF RECKONING & RETRIBUTION” was coming. Two days later, he threatened to invoke the Insurrection Act unless Minnesota officials stopped the supposed “professional agitators and insurrectionists” confronting ICE.

Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem confirmed that military intervention had been discussed. And by January 18, the Pentagon had placed roughly 1,500 active-duty soldiers on prepare-to-deploy orders. The administration was preparing the ground for deploying the military.

Nor do we have to guess how some White House officials hoped events would unfold. On January 17, Zeteo reported that two administration officials acknowledged that figures inside the White House would welcome significant violence by Minneapolis protesters. One senior official said they “would not mind it” if such violence provided a pretext for invoking the Insurrection Act.
In other words, widespread disorder wouldn’t have been a setback for Trump’s strategy. It could have provided exactly the excuse he needed.

The logic was straightforward: Provoke confrontations through extraordinary federal aggression. Wait for enraged protesters and community members to retaliate with widespread violence or property destruction. Then portray the movement as an anarchic threat to public safety, rally Americans around the need for order, and justify an unprecedented expansion of federal military power.

Recent revelations make the administration’s methods even more disturbing. As Wired reported this week, federal investigators infiltrated activist organizations and communications networks on an extraordinary scale. Attorney Kevin Riach, representing one of fifteen Minnesota activists facing federal charges, has argued in court that undercover agents participated in organizing groups while seeking to entice participants into criminal activity.

The strategy was hardly irrational. Research shows that property destruction, even on a limited scale, can sharply undermine public support for protests. It would not have taken much for Trump to transform a confrontation about federal repression into a national argument about supposedly violent leftists and blue-city disorder.

Imagine the aftermath of Good’s killing had Minneapolis descended into sustained rioting, widespread vandalism, and attacks on ICE or local police. How long before the national conversation shifted away from the shooting itself toward whether Trump should restore order and whether movements should oppose property destruction and violence?

header.h2: Why Minneapolis Didn’t Take the Bait

div.p: Trump’s central miscalculation wasn’t underestimating the anger his agents would generate. It was choosing to stage this provocation in one of the most deeply organized progressive metropolitan areas in the United States.

Minnesota has a rich, decades-long tradition of labor, immigrant-rights, and religious organizing. Groups including Unidos MN, ISAIAH, Service Employees International Union (SEIU) Local 26, and the Twin Cities teachers’ unions had spent years developing relationships, training leaders, winning reforms, and building the capacity to act together. As SEIU Local 26 President Greg Nammacher explained, their January resistance would not have succeeded without years of preparation: “We would not have met it if we had not built a capacity beforehand.”

These organizations saw clearly that a violent confrontation on Trump’s terms was one the movement was likely to lose. As JaNaé Bates Imari, co–executive director of the faith-based organization ISAIAH, explained in an interview on The Dig:

blockquote.p: Part of what is happening in Minnesota is a needling by the federal government to try to get us to respond in a particular way. And Minnesotans across the spectrum have said we will not take the bait . . . . No one [is] confused about who the peacekeepers are in the midst of what’s taking place.

div.p: Crucially, organizers went beyond merely preaching restraint by building the organizational capacity to turn restraint into a collective practice.

Unidos developed mass trainings for legal observation of ICE operations, ultimately training approximately thirty thousand people. ISAIAH trained hundreds of clergy, while allied groups trained thousands in nonviolent civil disobedience. Neighborhood Signal chats sprang up. Residents organized to document immigration raids, distribute whistles, support families sheltering at home, and mobilize neighbors.

There were genuine pressures toward escalation. Some protesters threw objects at officers, and instances of vandalism occurred. After witnessing federal violence, not everyone agreed about the limits of confrontation.

But breaking with unstrategic leftist norms about a “diversity of tactics,” the movement’s leading organizations had developed the relationships and legitimacy needed to establish collective norms about disciplined nonviolent mass action. The Minnesota Star Tribune reported that protesters confronted a suspicious flag-burner and that participants in organizing chats rebuked and expelled people proposing violence.

By cultivating shared expectations, training participants, challenging provocations, and giving people effective alternatives, the Minneapolis movement provided opponents of ICE with something more powerful to do than express their fury.

On January 23, an estimated 75,000 or more people marched through downtown Minneapolis in subzero weather during the Day of Truth and Freedom strike action. According to organizers, roughly a thousand businesses, overwhelmingly small businesses, participated in the work stoppage.

The movement’s militant resistance and discipline helped keep the attention on federal agents’ terrorization of Minneapolis’s undocumented community, as well as the heroism of two innocent Americans who decided to stand up for their neighbors.

Renée Good and Alex Pretti were ordinary people who resisted injustice and paid with their lives. But their deaths alone would not necessarily have been enough to defeat the administration’s offensive. Because without an organized movement committed to preventing mass violence and property destruction, their killings could have become entangled in a debate over which side was responsible for the disorder. Instead, Trump lost control of events and the narrative.
We don’t have to rely entirely on hypothetical scenarios to see what might have happened otherwise.

France’s growing protests this fall against the cost of living and the government have recently provided a troubling counterexample. What began with high school students protesting deteriorating educational conditions in September grew into a broader movement drawing in unions, Yellow Vests, and other groups demanding economic and political change.

But on October 17, huge demonstrations across the country were accompanied by extensive violence and destruction. Shops were looted in Paris, public buildings attacked, and Marseille’s city hall vandalized.

Remarkably, Le Monde reported that the government had deployed only about sixty thousand police nationwide — tens of thousands fewer than normal — even though intelligence services had warned of a high risk of violence and looting.

Before October 17, much of the national discussion had focused on police repression and the legitimacy of the protesters’ grievances. Afterward the government seized the opportunity to recast the confrontation as a battle against disorder. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu attacked the radical-left La France Insoumise, while politicians on the Right demanded harsher policing.

The events on October 17 were a gift to the right. Far-right leader Marine Le Pen received the most positive assessments of any major political figure’s response. And an Ipsos survey found that 55 percent of French respondents believed the leftist party La France Insoumise had contributed to the tensions and violence.

As historian Luca Provenzano has argued, allowing disorder to spread can itself be a highly effective state strategy. During France’s May 1968 upheaval, for example, authorities shifted from highly visible repression toward a more restrained police posture that created space for student escalation. A subsequent Interior Ministry assessment concluded that protesters’ excesses had helped restore support for order. The Right went on to win a sweeping electoral victory.

Whether the French government deliberately allowed the October 2026 violence to unfold is not yet established. But the danger doesn’t depend on proving a grand conspiracy. A state can benefit from disorder whether it consciously encourages it or simply takes advantage when it erupts. That’s precisely the trap Minneapolis avoided.

Of course, Trumpism is far from defeated. We don’t know exactly how badly MAGA will lose on Tuesday, and even a decisive electoral rebuke won’t automatically stop his political prosecutions, authoritarian ambitions, or continued mass deportations.

Trump could still try to manipulate or reject unfavorable election results, whether next week or in 2028. He could again seek to provoke widespread disorder and use the ensuing fear to justify repression.

To defeat Trumpism nationwide and to transform our country, we’ll need big, durable, welcoming organizations, new recruits beyond the ranks of existing college-educated activists, trusted leaders, and the ability to launch rapid, disciplined nonviolent action when necessary.

The best way to honor Renée Good and Alex Pretti — and to thank the people of Minneapolis for their courage and sacrifice — is to learn from what they achieved. Mass nonviolent resistance doesn’t happen automatically. It has to be organized. And when it is, even the most powerful government on earth can be forced to retreat.

entry.title: Socialists Need Our Own Foreign Policy Agenda

div.p: It is common for mainstream news outlets and political commentators in the United States to describe socialists as “very liberal” or simply “progressive,” or to puzzle over how to draw ideological lines between democratic socialists and others on the broad Left. There are, in fact, serious differences — differences that socialists would do well to sharpen and articulate for the public. At the same time, as the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) grows by leaps and bounds, some commentators prefer to highlight those DSA positions that are furthest from common agreement.

I have previously tried to distinguish between socialists and liberals when it comes to domestic economic policy. But what about foreign policy? Here I propose a socialist agenda for this field. Again, one of my objectives is to show how a socialist approach would differ from a liberal one when it comes to US relations with other countries.

As socialists work their way into positions of governing power in the United States in the form of urban mobilizations and the growth of the Squad and the DSA-allied bloc in Congress, we could expect the organs of “national security” to be among the last to open up. Historically, they have enjoyed considerable autonomy and have been the least susceptible to democratic accountability. The ease with which presidents of both parties have launched armed hostilities against other countries without the approval of the Congress, rumored to be a constitutional prerogative, has become notorious. Still, with growing political power will come opportunities for the Left to play a serious role in foreign policy.

header.h2: Understanding US Foreign Policy Since World War II

div.p: There was a moment in the 1970s when the fabled Church Committee exposed an endless series of dirty deeds committed by the Central Intelligence Agency, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, and others. That exposé was in 1975–76, and Senator Frank Church hailed from Idaho — these days as far right as a state can get.

Going back further, there was a moment in 1956 when a Republican president, Dwight D. Eisenhower, blocked US support for British and French imperialist machinations against Egypt after it nationalized the Suez Canal, which was surely Egypt’s right. Other than these anomalies, however, US-led Western imperialism has enjoyed free rein since World War II.

The basic dilemma for the Left is that the good deeds we might hope for our government to perform with the aid of its military would be the responsibility of a state that gives no sign of interest in beneficent acts. A libertarian friend impressed upon me the inevitability that any intervention by the (capitalist) state would be poisoned by craven, ulterior motives.

My thesis is that the overriding ulterior motive in US foreign policy since World War II has been world hegemony, enshrined in the infamous George Kennan “X Article,” which has superseded narrower economic concerns. It is this to which the quasi-autonomous institutions of US national security have been dedicated, hastening to fill the gaps left by the dissolution of the British and French empires.

Liberalism is compromised by sympathy for the hegemonic imperative. One notorious example was given by President Bill Clinton’s secretary of state, Madeleine Albright, who referred to the United States as “the indispensable nation.” In other words, hegemony was essential.

Another Democratic foreign policy maven and former human rights activist Samantha Power played the genocide card in her celebrated book, A Problem from Hell, to argue for a more interventionist US foreign policy. But when hell settled over Gaza and Ms Power had a chance to say something, her response to the carnage in 2024 was to send tents.

The Biden administration fiddled while Gaza was being blown to smithereens. It also dithered on the revival of Barack Obama’s deal with Iran, which likely made it easier for Donald Trump to initiate hostilities with the country when he returned to office. Of course, under the George W. Bush administration, we had the flaming lies about “weapons of mass destruction” (WMDs) in Iraq, now being replayed in absurdist form by President Trump with regard to Iran. Meanwhile, the US withdrawal from Iraq has left that field open to our supposed enemy, Iran. Nobody said foreign policy had to make sense.

The narrower, default stance on the Left has been blanket opposition to military intervention by the United States or its allies. The posture of liberal pro-interventionists is to exaggerate the horrors of a failure to intervene. These justifications have usually been spurious. Historically, every assault by a great power is justified by claims, usually fallacious, of a prior injury or of an overriding humanitarian purpose.

Complicating the picture, there are ways a powerful nation can commit aggression against a weaker one without resorting to military means. One has been the predatory use of indebtedness, about which much has been written. Another is the imposition of sanctions on the movement of capital and trade goods. The current weapon of choice is the tariff, not to mention the actual, lethal use of force by the United States and Israel currently on display in the Middle East. The effectiveness of sanctions and tariffs is open to question. And now the Trump administration is discovering in Iran that even its military might cannot always wrest concessions from a recalcitrant government.

Socialists, given the opportunity, would at the very least place a high bar before any proposals for US military intervention. We must reject the default to liberal excuses that skirt the underlying motivations for aggression. We saw many of these in the debates about Iraq: The Bush administration would not competently prosecute the war. The search for WMDs should have been allowed to continue. We failed to gain the cooperation of allies. Bush failed to get the proper approval from Congress.

Now the critique of choice is that “President Trump has no plan”; we also see efforts to use the spike in gas prices to score political points. We should be wary of putative anti-Trump voices with thin critiques of the Iran attacks. The issue is not the lack of an end game, Israeli connivance in the war, the shifting excuses for objectives, or the carnival of MAGA national security leaders.

And Trump does in fact have a plan: it is to flex, blow things up, kill people, and pose as the second coming of Douglas MacArthur. It may seem to boil down to the president’s deranged personality and feeble intellect, but the fact is that the US foreign policy establishment, guiding both parties, has had Iran in its sights for decades, ever since the rise of Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddegh in the 1950s and later the fall of the US puppet regime led by the shah.

War-skeptical liberals hoping for criticism of Trump’s Iran adventure from less militaristic US allies have been disappointed by the repetition of the bankrupt mantra that Iran must be blocked from possession of nuclear weapons. The allies have also been weak in their criticism of the machinations of Trump and the Israeli state in the Middle East, much like centrist or corporate Democrats in the United States.

One theory for US aggression that is bandied around is the notion that the international reserve currency status of the dollar would be endangered by oil exporters such as Iraq or Iran. But world trade is already conducted in a variety of currencies, not just the dollar, and this will increasingly be the case as the rest of the world — particularly the People’s Republic of China — continues to grow economically compared to the United States. Nations with large stocks of dollars also face the dilemma that if the dollar declines in value, which would happen if they tried to reduce their holdings in favor of another currency, their own wealth would take a hit.

Reductive economic explanations have plagued left-wing foreign policy debates more broadly for a long time. Back in the day, it was suggested that the Vietnam War was about the quest for control of rubber exports from Southeast Asia. In Kosovo, there was talk of vast mineral resources for which Western powers lusted. With Afghanistan, it was said that a pipeline was really what was at issue.

Now everything is supposed to be about oil. This may be so for Trump himself, but we know he is ignorant. The relevance of oil can be exaggerated. First, the world is weaning itself off fossil fuels, since wind, solar, and even nuclear can be more economical and secure. Second, the United States itself is a net exporter of fossil fuel. Third, much oil extraction sits uneasily on a knife-edge of profitability: a limited shift in its world price puts the higher-cost extraction operations out of business, which naturally limits investment. And fourth, investment in new extraction takes time and is prey to large, up-front, fixed costs that become sunk costs. Investment in oil and gas extraction is discouraged by the obstacles and uncertainties noted above; it can’t be turned on and off like a spigot.

This classic economic explanation for US aggression has been given new life by Trump’s nakedly acquisitive Venezuelan venture. We should not doubt that commercial opportunities existed in all of the targets of US interventions, including opportunities for fossil fuel exploitation. But the politics of hegemony, behind which stand the broad interests of capital, looms above them all. This basic analytical framework distinguishes socialists from liberals.

Today Donald Trump seems to have reduced the overarching, historic priority of Western imperialist hegemony, strongly founded in economic factors, to his personal dominance, wealth, and unrestrained freedom of action. We still lack a comprehensive story that explains the current regime, other than loose talk about nutty billionaires who want to go to Mars. Perhaps their influence, along with that of crypto bros, Gulf monarchs, and Israel’s rampages, exercise more leverage on Trump and US foreign policy than ordinarily understood.

We could imagine exceptions to default anti-interventionism. The big one now is Ukraine. Nobody proposes to send North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) troops up against Russians in Ukraine, but other types of assistance have been supported. I won’t try to resolve the Ukraine aid debate here, except to claim that there is a legitimate anti-Russian-imperialist rationale for aid. Socialists will probably remain divided on this question. There is a thin line between sending Ukraine missiles and sending US soldiers to fight alongside Ukrainians. (I don’t doubt the latter is also in progress, sub rosa, in the form of quasi-official trainers and operators.)

The broader issue is the fate of Europe, threatened on one side by the Russian Federation and on the other by Trump’s disdain for the NATO alliance. Europe is the chief redoubt of social democracy in the world, with all its faults, in sharp contrast to neofascist trends in Russia, India, Turkey, Hungary, Israel, the Philippines, and the United States itself. The fixation of the Left on NATO tends to gloss over this fact. Europe might also be considered a preferable rival for US hegemony; it would certainly be an improvement over Trumpist governance.

The other elephant in the room is Israel. By now the case for a liberal, much less a socialist, Zionism is dead. There can be no arguing about a death toll of seventy-thousand-plus, with a count that grows with new atrocities every day. The political collapse of Labor Zionism opens the way for a recovery of the history of Bundism, celebrated in the fabulous new book by Molly Crabapple.

header.h2: The Right to Self-Determination and Its Limits

div.p: A common theme for Ukraine, Palestine, and Iran is the right of a people to self-determination. This is a principle socialists ought to keep at the forefront; it was good enough for V. I. Lenin. Socialists have always been pioneers in the furtherance of democratic rights in capitalist countries, and democratic rights in domestic affairs logically extend to democracy in foreign policy — hence national self-determination. We may not like how some nations exercise such rights, but we often regret how other individuals exercise their freedoms, too. That doesn’t mean we are against freedom.

If an imperial hegemon is going to be meddling in affairs outside its borders, it should be limited to sending money and material assistance where it is needed, without conditions. In Ukraine, we could say that nation’s right to self-determination overrides concerns over the dangers of US-centric hegemony. In any case, the chief beneficiary of support for Ukraine is Europe.

An implication of the right of nations to self-determination, which in principle would logically, unavoidably apply to Israel, is the rightful sovereignty of nations. The dark side of sovereignty is the implied freedom of national governments to commit crimes against their own residents. There can also be a collision of national self-determinations, again vividly illustrated in Israel versus Palestine, so the principle cannot be an absolute one. But it can’t be ignored either. Israel has arguably forfeited its right to self-determination, just as could have been said of Cambodia under the Khmer Rouge.

One good rationale for the rights of nations and peoples (among which I would include Palestine) to be free from aggression is for the sake of world peace. I would designate peace the second socialist principle for foreign policy. Socialists like peace; the working class always bears the greatest costs of war.

Once military force is put to the side, the other sorts of economic aggression can be dealt with by diplomacy. Setting aside how Trump’s addled mind conceives of them, tariffs are ideally a device to more fairly apportion high value-added manufacturing, which every country seeks, among nations. So too can disagreements that lead to sanctions be resolved, short of the use of force.

Predatory international lending can be reformed. Debts can be relieved and payments rescheduled on more bearable terms, or canceled outright. Support for international institutions of diplomacy and aid such as the United Nations, which Trump is trying to supplant with his “Board of Peace,” can be strengthened. Most of this is consistent with a liberal perspective, but that doesn’t make it useless.

Regarding tariffs, liberals tend to swing against the working class in favor of a mythical “free trade.” For socialists, tariffs ought to serve a fair trade agenda that assists economic development in the poorer nations and promotes economic sustainability, especially with respect to climate change.

One debatable off-ramp from foreign policy liberalism is the so-called realist school in international relations. In recent years, the most visible public faces of this thinking have been John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt, mostly for their bracing criticism of Israel and the Zionist lobby. Yet underlying “realism” is a chauvinistic, foundational prioritizing of US national security — hence it is not a suitable framework for socialists.

The realists do tend to have better arguments than liberals, as the latter are caught between the impulse to do good deeds and the realities of national power. The realists’ skepticism and hardheadedness about military adventurism have been more persuasive. This restraint could prove to be reversed, however, in the case of escalated conflict with China, which is an unambiguous rival to the United States for superpower status.

International working-class solidarity is my proposal for a third basic socialist principle of foreign policy. But that idea is bedeviled in the near term by the reality that presently workers rely on their own governments for security. In that light, the straightforward posture is to stand for national self-determination, which means noninterventionism and peace.

Liberals tend to be animated by a desire to see the government right wrongs elsewhere. Consequently, they are suckered by appeals for humanitarian interventions. They are also reluctant to call a crackpot excuse an outright falsehood motivated by bad intentions. And out of patriotic reservations, they gloss over foreign policies rooted in exploitative economic schemes. They have yet to figure out the disastrous trend, not least for Jews themselves, in Zionism. (Some on the Right have, it seems: former US Ambassador to South Africa Patrick Gaspard pointed out that there was no resignation from the Biden administration over Gaza equivalent to the recent protest by the MAGA neofascist Joe Kent.)

In this respect, socialists, going against stereotype, are often much more realistic about government and politicians. Liberals are the dreamers, and US foreign policy is the nightmare from which we all have to wake up.

The three basic socialist principles of national self-determination, peace, and international working-class solidarity offer a way out. The liberal, on the other hand, is caught between patriotic hopes for humanitarian interventionism, invariably dashed, and a desire for peace; they also fail to reckon with the relevance of trade policy to working-class interests. Incidentally, trade policy could conceivably benefit workers in the countries of our trade partners by upholding labor-rights components of trade agreements, a purpose for which liberals are usually asleep at the wheel.

It seems possible that socialist principles for foreign policy would even have some currency among Trump voters. The divisions among them over the Iran war are well known. Their neo-isolationism dovetails with socialist opposition to the hegemonic imperative, not to mention “forever wars.” Neither is the Democrats’ embrace of free trade doing them any good among working-class Trump voters.

The biggest obstacle to a peace-oriented foreign policy is the susceptibility of voters of all political types to paranoia. For that, a ready antidote is at hand: the manifest, recent failures of bipartisan-cum-Trumpian foreign policy in Libya, Syria, Iraq, and Iran. Aside from the usual, scandalous neglect of ongoing genocides in Africa and Palestine, the key fact undermining the usual US foreign policy nostrums is that its adventurism has failed in its own terms.

entry.title: A Palestinian Prisoner on the Nightmare Behind Israeli Bars

div.p: Born in Nablus in 1963, Khalida Jarrar is one of the foremost voices of the Palestinian left — feminist, secular, socialist — and one of the towering figures of the political prisoners’ movement. For more than a decade she led Addameer, the main Palestinian prisoner support organization. In 2006, voters elected her to the Palestinian Legislative Council, where she chaired the prisoners’ commission, and she later served on the national committee that prepared Palestine’s accession to the International Criminal Court. Today she is a researcher at the Muwatin Institute at Birzeit University, where she is conducting a pioneering study of the class and gender dimensions of the women prisoners’ movement since 1967.

She has paid for each of these roles with her own freedom. Israel has imprisoned her five times, for a total of more than six years behind bars. Almost every time, Israel held her under “administrative detention,” a system it inherited from British colonial emergency law. It allows indefinite imprisonment on the basis of a “secret file,” without charge, without trial, and without a lawyer able to contest what cannot be read.

In 2014, when the Israeli army ordered Jarrar’s expulsion from Ramallah to Jericho, she refused and lived for a month in a protest tent until the order fell. In 2015, twelve charges against her amounted to political acts: speeches, attending a book fair, and visiting a released prisoner. In 2021, during yet another detention, her daughter Suha, a thirty-one-year-old researcher, died suddenly — and Israel denied her mother a farewell.

Israeli forces arrested her for the fifth time in the early hours of December 26, 2023, the day before she was due to publicly present a study on Israel’s abuses against Palestinian prisoners during the genocide in Gaza. Thirteen months of administrative detention followed. She spent the last six in total isolation, in a cell two and a half meters by one, without a window or ventilation. Prison authorities moved her there days after Israel’s national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, visited Damon Prison.
When she asked why, a guard replied: “You will not know the reason for your isolation, nor how long it will last.” She walked out on January 19, 2025, in the first prisoner exchange of the ceasefire.

The conversation below took place in English, in mid-August. Israel’s doctrine of destroying refugee camps is spreading from the northern West Bank to the gates of Jerusalem. Israel voted in legislative elections on October 27, and Palestinians face elections in November that many do not believe in. Against this backdrop, Jarrar talks about prisons and libraries, about imperialism and oxygen — and about what a person does, locked alone in a darkened cell, in order not to go mad.

dt.p: Jacobin

Israel first arrested you on March 8, 1989 — International Women’s Day, at the height of the first intifada. In an essay, you begin the history of the prisoners’ movement not with a battle but with a song: the women of the 1936 revolt who, outside the British Mandate’s prisons, hid messages in coded syllables of folk songs. You also trace an unbroken legal line from British colonial emergency laws to today’s military courts — and Israel has detained around one million Palestinians since 1967, more than fifty thousand of them children. How do you explain that an emergency law older than the Universal Declaration of Human Rights is still, in 2026, putting people in cells without charge?

dd.p: Khalida Jarrar

When we talk about the colonial system, we have to talk about the colonial system all over the world. In the case of Palestine, there is a direct continuity with the British system: the British Mandate governed through emergency laws — house demolitions, curfews, collective punishment, administrative detention. When Israel came, it continued that system, learned from it, developed it — and today it exports it across the whole world. We are talking about a system tied to all the capitalist and imperial systems.

Since 1967, around one million Palestinians have passed through Israeli prisons, including children and women. And the prison system is the same as under the mandate. In my research, I found that it is also very similar to the Irish experience and to the US system.

It is a colonial system that always seeks the same thing — to colonize, to settle. Within its liberal mechanism, it developed something I call “making it nice”: making violence presentable through the law, through emergency laws, through military orders. That is why administrative detention exists: they arrest anyone on the basis of a so-called secret file, and there are people who spend seven years like that, without anyone ever accusing them of anything.

This struggle against colonial emergency laws no longer belongs only to Palestinians — they have become a worldwide mechanism, and we have to fight them together. And when we turn to international humanitarian law, we find that Israel has violated it in its entirety: the right to life, the conventions on the treatment of prisoners, the right to a fair trial. There is a big question today about this system: Is international law for the weak or an excuse for the strong? I believe we need an international law for the victims, not for the colonial system — a global system in the service of the weak and of the victims to protect, in the end, humanity.

dt.p: Jacobin

Israel holds more than 9,600 Palestinian political prisoners today, over 3,500 of them without charge and some 350 of them children. More than one hundred have died in custody. Israel bars the International Committee of the Red Cross from visiting, and a new law creates a special court for Palestinians, with the death penalty. You came out of six months of solitary confinement straight into freedom and said that conditions are the worst since 1967 — that Ben-Gvir, Israel’s minister of national security, “treats prisoners as if they were not human.” What has changed?

dd.p: Khalida Jarrar

In my last imprisonment, I spent thirteen months in administrative detention, six of them in isolation. Ben-Gvir’s policy uses the tools of punishment out loud, not under the table. And he is proud when he enters prisoners’ cells to threaten them. He is proud of the death penalty law — when the world is moving to abolish that punishment, because it is inhuman.

He has reopened cells and prisons that Israel had closed for decades. In Ramle there is an underground prison, the “Rakevet,” which Israel used from 1967 until the mid-1970s and then shut down, because it was too terrible. Ben-Gvir reopened it and put people from Gaza there. For Gaza’s prisoners, there is in fact a kind of administrative detention called the “unlawful combatants” law: six months, renewable for another six, and another six, with no one knowing until when.

From my own experience, I tell you: they treat you like an animal. They attack your humanity — they want you to feel that you are not a human being. I do not want to go into details about the food, the beatings, the strip searches, the punishments.

But imagine: six months in a cell two and a half meters by one, with no windows, in summer, full of humidity. For the first three months the light was always on; then they started switching it off during the day and keeping it on all night. There was no oxygen.

This punishment is revenge, because I did nothing but give some speeches about the political situation. Of course I am Palestinian, I am against the occupation, and I seek the freedom of my people, as I seek the freedom of all the peoples of the world — I believe in that connection. And anyone who lives under the capitalist system also knows the mechanisms that crush people: running to eat, running for a house, living only to survive. What they did to me is a small example of how this system, full of violence, treats people in an inhuman way.

dt.p: Jacobin

Those who study incarceration — in Palestine and around the world — say that solitary confinement is not an extra degree of harshness: it is a distinct instrument that works by removing the collective Palestinian prisoners spent sixty years building. The question is not how you endured the pain — it is how you kept your political mind intact, your mental health, when they took away exactly the thing that makes it political. And one more: the late prisoner and writer Walid Daqqah wrote that the occupier had moved on from disciplining bodies to trying to dismantle consciousness itself. Is that what you felt they were trying to do to you?

dd.p: Khalida Jarrar

Yes, of course — that is their aim. From the first moment I entered isolation, which is an extremely hard experience, I made two decisions. The first: how to make my body survive; the second: how to keep my mind working. Because their aim is for you to go mad, or to damage your thinking.

The body I saved with water — drinking water, the only thing I had. And sometimes they cut it off, as punishment: two or three days without water, without being able to shower. Sometimes they brought me a bottle; other times they “forgot” — because the essential thing is to negate you, to pretend you are not there. When the guards passed the door of my cell, they turned their faces away; they did not look at me.
The mind was the second battle. In those few meters, I walked all day long. I decided not to sleep during the day — only at night.

There were no books; there was nothing inside the cell. So I held discussions inside my head. I told myself: they want to destroy you, but you are part of a people fighting for its freedom, and you are part of the strugglers of the whole world — like Bobby Sands, like Angela Davis. You belong to those people.

And I worked. At Birzeit University, I am doing a major piece of research on the class and gender analysis of women prisoners from 1967 until today — I had already written parts of it. So I would discuss the research with myself.

And there is something else: what they did shows their fascism, but it does not make me a victim. I am not an individual; I believe in the collective experience. That is why when people tell me, “we want to write your story,” I answer: no. I write about the collective experience because we are part of a collective experience worldwide.

The root of the fascist capitalist system contains violence. Violence is part of its content — not freedom and democracy, which are the slogans they want to teach us. Lately I have gone back to reading Karl Marx’s Capital, the pages on the violence of the colonial systems, on how many people they killed.
That is how I governed myself inside: always believing that I am part of a whole, that I am not alone. Those were the words I used with myself: Khalida, you are not alone.

dt.p: Jacobin

The activist Munther Amira tells this story: when Israeli authorities transferred him to a high-security prison, he found in the yard a thin, weakened man he barely recognized who called out his name. It was Marwan Barghouti. The next day, the prisoners were sitting in a circle listening to Barghouti give a lecture — because the guards had emptied the prison library, and the men had answered by teaching one another.

Barghouti pointed him to a chair: “It’s your turn. We want to hear about your nonviolent resistance.” And when they asked him what he thought of it, he replied: “Call it whatever you like, as long as you resist.” Later, Barghouti sent word, through his wife, that Amira should come back to prison for another six months, to give more lectures.

You did precisely this on the women’s side — and wrote it down: “We are transforming the prison into a school.” The censors let in Ghassan Kanafani, Maxim Gorky, and Davis — and never let in [Antonio] Gramsci. How does that world work, from the inside? And why does the jailer fear an Italian intellectual who has been dead for almost ninety years?

dd.p: Khalida Jarrar

When Israel arrested me in 2015, there were twenty-three of us women in prison. Most were under eighteen, students — and some were facing heavy sentences: ten, fifteen years. I began to think that education was essential for them: so that they would not spend those ten years merely inside a cell.
We discussed how to do it: first a small school, then a university. Seven women finished their studies and, after their release, are now doing their master’s degrees.

We ran into two problems: first, there were no books; second, the official conditions required two women with master’s degrees to teach — and at that moment I was the only woman in the prison with a master’s. At that time it was still possible to discuss matters through the lawyers, and our families visited us — that ended after October 7, 2023.

And there was an opportunity: the prison for underage boys was next to ours, and the prison authorities decided to transfer the boys to other prisons. Through the women’s representative, we got them to leave us their library — with the official schoolbooks. They moved us into the boys’ section, and the books stayed.

But we thought: they may come and confiscate them at any moment. So we copied the books by hand, in full. We divided the responsibility — each woman copied a part. We had pencils and notebooks, and we began.

Through the lawyers we reached the Palestinian Ministry of Education, which agreed to recognize me officially as a teacher. We gave classes in which we tied study to life — theory with practice. And we succeeded: they took the exam and finished high school. Before my release, I chose two women, showed them how we worked, and prepared them to continue.

The dream of those serving life sentences was university — imprisoned men studied at university; the women, never. After my release, I went to discuss it with the minister of higher education. They told me: “three master’s holders are required.”
I answered: What are we to do, if women with master’s degrees are not in prison? It is the men who seem clever to you . . . [laughs] We agreed on a method to get around the problem.
And then Israel arrested me again. Do you know what the women told me? “We are sad that you are in prison again — but, in here, we are happy: we can continue our studies. And we like you.”
That is what Barghouti sent word to Amira for: come back, we want to continue the classes. The prisoners want their teachers back.

[Laughs.] We succeeded. At that time, the prison authorities allowed each woman three books a month, which our families brought in. The guards always searched them, and the censors always read them. And Gramsci they always confiscated; they never let Gramsci in.

dt.p: Jacobin
Why?

dd.p: Khalida Jarrar

I don’t know — it is a question I ask myself, not them: Are you afraid of Gramsci? He died so long ago. They let in Davis — alive, a critic of the prison system, an active voice for Palestine. The dead Italian, no.

dt.p: Jacobin

Let us talk about the Palestinian political situation. The polls are brutal: around 80 percent of Palestinians want Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas gone. Barghouti leads every presidential poll from his cell; elections are due on November 28, and 60 percent do not believe they will take place.

In 2016, you said that elections within the existing framework “will solve nothing” — that the root lies in the Palestine National Council and the refoundation of the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO). Do you stand by that? And security coordination with Israel: Can the Palestinian Authority reform it, or only end it?

dd.p: Khalida Jarrar

If we need elections, we need real elections — not elections that the European Union, the Americans, and the Israelis design to shape the system to what they want. They want, for example, a system without the political parties that did not accept the Oslo Accords. Look at what happened in the municipal elections: Israel interfered directly — they phoned people to say, “if you stand as a candidate, you will be arrested.” And they arrested many.

We need elections that give the Palestinian people the right to decide, not the United States, nor Israel, nor the European Union deciding for the Palestinians. And it is from that perspective that I believe in the refoundation of the PLO: through elections to the Palestine National Council, not to the Legislative Council. Today no free elections are possible: they interfere with the candidates, they want to shape the Palestinian system to their will. That is why I do not think it will go well.

dt.p: Jacobin

Let me end with the paradox of this moment. The Palestinian cause has never been so popular in the West: for the first time in a quarter of a century, Americans sympathize more with Palestinians than with Israel; some 160 states recognize Palestine. Zohran Mamdani is mayor of New York City. Rashida Tlaib and Ilhan Omar sit in Congress.

Abdul El-Sayed won a Senate primary in Michigan against $30 million of pro-Israel money. Catherine Connolly won Ireland’s presidency with Palestine at the heart of her campaign. Rima Hassan, born in a refugee camp, is a member of the European Parliament. And yet European arms and trade keep flowing, while British police arrest thousands under terrorism laws for holding a placard.
From Damon, you wrote in 2020 that these gestures of solidarity “empower us, prisoners, from within.” What do you ask of this elected generation abroad?

dd.p: Khalida Jarrar
I dream of a new world. And I think the changes are coming: good changes. What you describe in the United States are changes at the root.

We have not yet reached the point where things collapse, but these accumulated changes become big changes. I think that, after the genocide, the world realized that this fascist genocide can also reach their own houses and their own cities.

That is why I believe, and I dream, that the world will change toward more justice, toward a real democracy, not this democracy. I dream, of course, of my people’s self-determination, of our freedom, without occupation. And I dream, for the whole world, of peace, real justice, and equality among all peoples.

And I hope that the socialist system will be the solution. I know that the practical experience, in some countries, did not work, but I believe in the ideas, and in how to make them live, because I believe in equality and in social justice.

entry.title: A Midterm Rout Will Hurt the GOP, but Trumpism Will Endure

div.p: Observers across the spectrum expect Democrats to make significant gains in the upcoming midterms, in House and Senate races and beyond. There are good reasons to trust in their predictions. Nonpresidential elections in the US are increasingly “nationalized,” meaning that evaluations of presidential and national politics strongly influence down-ballot choices. And President Donald Trump, having behaved cruelly and erratically while presiding over a weak economy and an unpopular war with Iran, has not set Republicans up for success.

With inflation rates high, wages stagnant, and borrowing costs elevated, economic issues are central to the GOP’s current quandary. In a recent Washington Post–ABC News–Ipsos poll, Trump’s economic approval rating stands at just 28 percent. By a three-to-one margin, respondents said the state of the economy was either not so good or poor. Forty-eight percent said they were financially worse off than when Trump returned to office in 2025, the highest percentage saying this about any president in Post-ABC polls since 1986. On other issues, 65 percent said it was a mistake to take military action against Iran, and 68 percent disapproved of the way Trump has dealt with US allies. Tellingly, 56 percent said Trump had gone too far in deporting undocumented immigrants, compared with 48 percent in April 2025.

But whatever happens in November, Trump will hold office for two more years, and the politics he represents won’t evaporate when he exits. Anyone expecting a midterm rout and Trump’s departure in 2029 to restore the old normal — and for the old normal to be sufficient to prevent another far-right resurgence — needs to think again. Instead, we must reckon with the political force that has been unleashed in American life, the aftershocks of which will no doubt be felt for generations to come.

In my new book, Class, Power and the State in the Trump Era: A Critical Analysis (De Gruyter Brill, 2026), I try to sketch an early picture of Trumpism. Below I draw on it to describe what Trumpism is made of, how it changed between Trump’s two terms, and what that means for the Left.

One unmistakable aspect of Trumpism is brazen authoritarianism. This dimension is on full display right now, as Trump works diligently to undermine confidence in the electoral system. The Supreme Court checked his attempt to use the US Postal Service to restrict mail-in ballots in September. Since then, the administration has engaged in “systematically laying out unsubstantiated and false claims in an effort to sow doubts about the safety of the country’s decentralized election system,” as a New York Times analysis put it.

For example, as part of Trump’s big-lie campaign about illegal voting, the Justice Department claimed without evidence that twenty thousand people on California’s voter rolls were “likely noncitizens.” The department then charged twenty-eight California residents, all legal immigrants, with violating federal election laws. Despite Trump’s disinformation campaign, most Americans are confident the midterm elections will be conducted fairly, though seven in ten lack confidence that Trump will accept the results if Republicans lose.

Recent weeks have brought stepped-up repression against those Trump regards as enemies. Most notably, Department of Homeland Security officials raided the Washington home of Congresswoman Ilhan Omar, the Somali American representative of Minnesota’s Fifth District, seizing her phone, passport, and other documents. Trump has long displayed a fixation on Omar, whom he has called “garbage,” and on Somali Americans, who reside in large numbers in Minnesota, especially in the Twin Cities area. Several days before the raid, Trump wrote on Truth Social, “The once Great State of Minnesota is being taken over by Somali Immigrants. There is Violence, Murder, and Mayhem all over the State. The people of Minnesota must fight back.” According to several reports, those familiar with the probe believe that its goal is to revoke Omar’s citizenship and eventually deport her.

In my book, I characterize Trumpism as a distinct form of right-wing politics, blending (pseudo-)populism, nationalism, and authoritarianism with uninhibited, even predatory or patrimonial, pro-capitalist economic and social policies. While these political forms have existed in various shapes throughout American political history, they combined in new ways in the Trump era. Trumpism marked a departure from the pre-2016 Republican ideological consensus and signaled the arrival of an alternative form of right-wing politics, one that played out in other countries as well.The goal of the MAGA movement is to weaken rival forces and establish hegemony in American politics based on a reconfigured national-conservative bloc enjoying both popular and elite support. The attack on the election system and the raid on Omar’s home make sense in that light. A movement bent on dominating American politics has every reason to discredit the elections that could check its power and to punish the people it treats as enemies.

If these features were plainly evident in Trump’s first presidency, they only deepened their hold after he left office in 2021 and during his second presidency. From 2021 to 2025, between Trump’s two terms, Trumpism underwent four important shifts. First, Trump’s reactionary political worldview grew more radical, marked by an unremitting commitment to the stolen-2020-election lie, intensifying authoritarianism, vows of retribution, and hysterical rhetoric about the threat of socialism, communism, and the “radical Left.”

Second, the Trump campaign worked with right-wing think tanks to draw up blueprints for a second Trump administration. The purpose was to go beyond such traditional conservative objectives as cutting taxes and reducing spending to a wholesale assault on the administrative state that would give the president complete control over the executive branch. As Russell Vought, now Trump’s budget director, put it in 2023, “The president Day One will be a wrecking ball for the administrative state.” The best-known plan for a second Trump administration was the Heritage Foundation’s Project 2025, released in 2023, of which Vought was a key architect.

Third, Trump and the MAGA movement aligned closely with the preoccupations of right-wing culture and political thought, such as Christian nationalism, anti-wokeness crusading, “pro-natalism,” and concerns about “civilizational erosion” that draw on the far-right great replacement theory. Such thinking is common among Trump 2.0 figures like JD Vance, Pete Hegseth, and Stephen Miller.

Fourth, after leaving office in 2021, Trump almost entirely abandoned the economic pseudo-populism aimed at the working class that was a prominent part of his 2016 campaign. Trump’s 2024 campaign openly courted Wall Street, Silicon Valley, and other parts of corporate America, such as oil and gas, tobacco, and the cryptocurrency industry, which he had previously called a scam.

Trump vowed to cut corporate tax rates, reduce environmental and other regulations, and support fossil fuel drilling. In May 2026, Trump was asked if “Americans’ financial situation” motivated him to make a deal with Iran. “Not even a little bit,” he replied. “I don’t think about Americans’ financial situation. I don’t think about anybody. I think about one thing — we cannot let Iran have a nuclear weapon. That’s all.” He added, “Every American understands.”

But not every American understands. The war with Iran is unpopular, especially in the context of Americans’ domestic economic difficulties. Those difficulties are largely of the president’s own making.

Trump’s signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act, enacted in July 2025, has been called “the most regressive tax and budget legislation in modern American history” by Yale scholars Patrick Sullivan and Jacob Hacker. The inflationary pressures squeezing the working class stem largely from misguided Trump policies, including the war on Iran, which has driven up the price of oil and oil-based products; across-the-board tariffs, which have raised prices of imported goods and inputs used in domestic production; and anti-immigration and deportation measures that have led to labor shortages in construction, agriculture, meatpacking, and other sectors.

So the conditions exist for a large-scale repudiation of Trump and the MAGA movement, which are increasingly authoritarian and even fascistic. As early as 1921, more than a year before the March on Rome, Antonio Gramsci theorized the cross-class, psychologically intense appeal of fascism, noting that fascism “has become an unleashing of elemental forces which cannot be restrained within the bourgeois system of economic and political governance.” The challenge for the Left is to construct a politics that can leash, redirect, and de-energize these “elemental forces” to forestall further drift toward authoritarianism and fascism, something centrist and corporate liberalism has been unable to do.

What does this mean for politics after the midterm elections? First, the Left needs educational efforts to counter McCarthyite attacks from the Right on progressive and socialist ideas so that they can be discussed rationally and without stigma. Second, it should build on the successful electoral work by the Democratic Socialists of America and other groups seen in the Zohran Mamdani campaign in New York and elsewhere. Third, it needs progressive populist economic plans that serve working-class interests and cut through right-wing pseudo-populism. Economist Isabella Weber’s proposals for strategic price controls, which have been discussed in Jacobin, are one starting point worth considering. Gains by the Left in areas such as these will help counter not just the remainder of the Trump 2.0 presidency but Trumpism as an increasingly malignant form of right-wing, antidemocratic capitalist politics.

entry.title: In Italy, Giorgia Meloni Is Hardening Her Calls for Order

div.p: There’s a story doing the rounds. A woman is sitting in a bar in tourist-filled Turin; you can imagine the glass panes looking out onto the square, the little tables for spritzes and olives. Kids and chitchat. Then, out of nowhere, everyone starts coughing and wheezing; she feels a burning sensation in her eyes. The air is filled with white fumes, tear gas engulfing the little tables. Everyone rushes inside, they lock themselves in. Only afterward do they spy, through the fumes, a few hooded protesters running towards the piazza. Only afterward — when they can breathe more easily and slip into the side streets to make their way home — are the squares and streets fully taken over by skirmishes and barricades.

The great Italian critical theorist Furio Jesi, thinking of his native Turin, wrote in 1969 that “you can love a city, and recognize its houses and its street in your deepest and dearest memories: but it’s only in the moment of revolt that you feel like the city is truly yours.” Revolts, Jesi argued, offer up strangely telling moments of symbolism. In the story above, the tear gas arrives before the protests. It smothers the emblematic scene of Italy’s commercial place in the world — its food and monuments, the great Italian hope. The image is engulfed by clouds of authoritarianism. The protesters arrive afterward, few and scattered, but the damage precedes them.

The protests that have rocked northern Italy over the past two weeks represent the outcome of years of repression and criminalization by the political and media classes. On the one hand, they take inspiration from a remarkably international moment. R., an activist from Cantiere — one of Milan’s historic social centers — tells me that young people of North African descent in Milan’s suburbs look to their French equivalents like their big brothers, with their expansive culture of hip-hop, film, and militancy. And similarly, she notes, throughout the street protests you could see not only the ubiquitous Palestinian flags, but also Moroccan and Albanian ones, symbols of other cousins in other streets but in the same struggle. On the other hand, interviews with kids involved in the clashes and protests in Milan and elsewhere underscore the desperation of Italy’s economic conditions: families that simply cannot get by on poverty wages. It is entirely normal in Italy for a month’s salary to be less than €1,000, barely covering rent and bills. Add to this the rising costs of food and gas, and it is surprising that the protests didn’t break out sooner.

While the windows of high-end shops caved in across the city centers in the north, supermarket shelves have been going empty across the south. Motorways and ports have been blocked by thousands of truckers striking against rising fuel costs — with the result that basic produce hasn’t been getting from farm to table. The self-employed truckers have found wide public support, M., an activist from Porco Rosso, a left-wing community center in Palermo, tells me. The social centers and grassroots trade unionists have been coming out to support, but also small business owners from the tourism industry as well as from across the agricultural sector. No fuel, no food and supplies, no business. Less economic miracle than economic mirage.

The government’s principle reaction to the protests has been to criminalize them. A few days after the aperitivi tables went flying in Turin, Giorgia Meloni announced that she would be pushing through a new law removing legal protections for young people, and establishing harsher sentencing. At the same time, thousands of truckers have been identified by police and hundreds served with fines for blocking the road. Searching for a scapegoat to offer up to the right-wing electorate, decolonial activist Youssef Siher was arrested on “terrorism” charges so fabricated that the courts immediately ordered his release. Giving short shrift to the separation of executive and judicial branches, Meloni attacked the judge’s decision as “shameful,” an affront to the police’s hard work.

Responding to protest with new criminal measures, mass arrests, and undermining the courts are standard elements in the repertoire of any right-wing government, not least in Italy. But these tactics have become a leitmotif of Meloni’s stint as prime minister in particular, for reasons that can be explained through a brief look back over the past five years of Italian politics.

Back in 2021, in the wake of the economic crash and burn of the plague biennial, the European Union once more installed a technocratic government to manage the billions in fiscal stimulus that was to be invested in the country’s economy. Capitalist powers were determined that the cash was not going to be wasted on handouts and kickbacks. Nearly all the main parties, including the hitherto ruling Democratic/Five Star alliance, backed Mario Draghi’s broad coalition, lining up behind the promise of a financial miracle. It was a disastrous political strategy. Only two parties stood out of line, Nicola Fratoianni’s Sinistra Italia (center left) and Meloni’s Fratelli d’Italia (far right). Casting itself as the underdog and riding a wave of racist anti-immigrant hatred, Meloni’s party picked up enough votes to become the largest single party.

Fast forward to 2026. The EU’s post-COVID stimulus money, predictably squandered in half-baked projects and through a chronic lack of civil service staffing, was directed to Italy more than any other country but failed to save it from stagnation. The result is not only that gas prices are soaring, but that the Italian state lacks the funds, and the will, to dig the working classes out of the hole it has plunged them into. Lacking the economic clout or courage to introduce policies that respond to grievances expressed across every part of society, the Meloni government has consistently turned to boasting about new laws to criminalize dissent.

The sheer range of activities and people targeted by the government through new laws and decrees over just four years is truly astounding. Ravers, anarchists, people smugglers, youth gangs, families employing surrogates, environmentalists, squatters, anti-Zionists, protesters in prisons, protesters in detention centers, the parents of protesters — and, of course, street protesters in general — have all been targets for new legislation threatening administrative fines or harshened prison sentences. To this growing list of subversives we can also add a whole series of criminal proceedings and investigations that have effectively been spearheaded by the government, against sea rescue missions, striking trade unionists, the Palestine solidarity movement, and, most recently, doctors supporting patients threatened with forced deportation.

The vast majority of these laws and investigations have not actually led to social activists and other rebels being given longer sentences or thrown in prison at a greater rate. This is largely thanks to the relative independence of the Italian courts (along with constant work by lawyers’ networks and solidarity movements), that have challenged these laws at every turn, often leading to pernicious reforms being blocked by judges. The government’s response has been to support a smear campaign against the “red robes” — i.e., left-leaning judges — culminating in March’s government-driven referendum to reform the judiciary. This led to the first real chink in Meloni’s public image, however: the reforms were voted down.

Despite the failure of the strategy on any practical level, the government has little to lean on by now except for such threats and rhetorical attacks. It came as little surprise, then, that the main response to the riots in the north and the strikes in the south was a wave of arrests (including schoolchildren arrested at the school gates), high-profile investigations, resurrection of the old boogeyman of “organized crime,” and the announcement of yet another security law.

Announcing the new law on TV, Meloni focused on the petty looting. “I want to be clear: no political ideal, no opposition to the government, justifies destroying a shop to make off with the goods. Behind that window there’s a family who has made lifelong sacrifices, workers who risk losing their jobs, citizens who have the right to experience their own city without fear.” But you can look through a window from two sides. From one side you see the commodities; from the other you look out to the street, where there are indeed workers, families and citizens — the very same people who form that grand litany of subjects that the government has threatened and bullied over the last four years. People who, in a moment of revolt, perhaps really did experience their city without fear.
The underlying causes of — and future prospects for — the current conflagrations cannot be separated from international politics, including Italy’s relationship to the United States.

If, in 2022, the watchwords had been the job market and the EU stimulus program, now they are the old couplet of fuel prices and global warfare. And though once a thorn in the EU’s side, it is now the Meloni government that has tried to appease European politicians and capitalist forces by backing the Israeli-US war against Iran and the genocide in Palestine — while also attempting to second guess Donald Trump’s military erraticism, whipping between support for Ukraine and Russia like a tattered flag in a storm.

The fuel dispute that has been burning all year strikes at the heart of the problems facing Italy and Italians. The US-Iraeli war on Iran has shot gas prices up by 25 percent since January. Attempting to soften the blow, the government’s response was to cut fuel taxes across the board, lowering the prices at the pump. This has been an extremely costly solution for a government desperately trying to avoid an EU infringement procedure: the fuel tax cuts cost the budget half a billion euros every month — which is why Meloni was winding the policy down, to the truckers’ ire.

That policy has now been replaced — thanks to the truckers’ wildcat strikes — by subsidies specifically aimed at supporting diesel-dependent businesses. While this may appease some of the more militant and organized logistics workers in the south, it does not provide a response to the impact of fuel costs more generally. Meloni is aware of this, and promptly flew to Kuwait to smooth out a deal on price capping fuel imports in exchange for military assistance to the US-allied petrostate.

Leveraging Italy’s geopolitical position to resolve economic problems at home has been Meloni’s horizon throughout her premiership. But, as I have argued before, the gamble hasn’t been paying off. In large part, this is because these alliances are being rejected by the electorate. Despite the opinions of the mainstream press and industrialists alike, Italians increasingly oppose arming Ukraine, and — as last year’s vast if ephemeral demonstrations proved — are generally supportive of Palestinian liberation. Much depends on the turnout for the upcoming national strikes by Italy’s small but militant grassroots Unione Sindacale di Base as well as the giant left-wing Confederazione Generale Italiana del Lavoro, both of which rightly demand higher salaries and criticize arms spending.

Still more, next year Italians will go to the polls. The Italian left has a historic opportunity: to unite around an internationalist antiwar platform and propose radical economic change that resolves the structural problems of Italian society — rather than knee-jerk policies that just shove cash into one worker’s hands while handcuffing another’s.
