entry.title: Livorno Dockworkers Are Trying to Block the Weapons of War

div.p: Livorno, Italy — “Sunaid X, Sunaid X, Sunaid X, this is Sumud, do you copy?”
“You’re calling Sunaid X.”
“Sunaid X, you are carrying supplies to a military base that is deeply involved in Zionists’ warfare and the genocide of the Palestinian people. The port is blocked for you. You’re not welcome here.”

So went last Thursday’s radio exchange between Global Sumud Flotilla (GSF) activist Luca Poggi and the bridge of the Sunaid X, a container ship that local unions had identified as a supplier of the NATO military base Sigonella, the US Navy’s air station in Sicily. After lying in wait for a week, living aboard three GSF sailboats at the port, around ten GSF members sprang into action midday on October 22.

img.alt: A Global Sumud Flotilla sailboat faces a Guardia di Finanza patrol boat at the mouth of Livorno’s harbor. Top right: The Sunaid X on the horizon off the Tuscan coast. Bottom right: Containers stacked behind a wall at the Port of Livorno. October 22, 2026.

figure.figcaption: A Global Sumud Flotilla sailboat faces a Guardia di Finanza patrol boat at the mouth of Livorno’s harbor. Top right: the Sunaid X on the horizon off the Tuscan coast. Bottom right: containers stacked behind a wall at the Port of Livorno. October 22, 2026. (Andrea Bellaroto)

div.p: According to a statement from Gruppo Autonomo Portuali (GAP), an autonomous collective of Livorno dockworkers, and the Unione Sindacale di Base (USB), an independent rank-and-file union that has led Livorno’s port blockades, the Sunaid X links Livorno with Sigonella for the US Defense Logistics Agency. The shipping vessel was due to load bulk chemicals, paints, food, and lithium batteries for drones at the Terminal Darsena Toscana (TDT).

Weather delays had already pushed back the Sunaid X’s arrival by two days. The ship missed its 2 p.m. Thursday berth at the TDT, Livorno’s main container terminal. Two of the sailboats held the harbor entrance, while the third took up position at the ship’s berth, and from roughly 2:30 to 8:30 p.m., the Sunaid X lay at anchor offshore. On land, USB called a strike, and GAP and USB picketed the terminal gate. When the ship finally docked that evening, dockworkers on the night shift refused to service it, and Friday’s morning shift did the same.

The Guardia di Finanza, Italy’s militarized financial and customs police, seized the three sailboats and held the GSF crews into the evening at a barracks beside the harbor master’s office. All ten were released late Thursday after being reported to prosecutors for “disruption of a public service,” an accusation that will go before a local judge, where the defendants will be represented by Tatiana Montella, a lawyer who works with GSF, according to the organization. The boats remain confiscated and under seizure.

A solidarity rally had gathered in the city that evening as the GSF activists were detained. “The boats of the Global Sumud Flotilla have led the way, and dockworkers have continued this fight on the docks, transforming solidarity into concrete action,” one protester told the local press. “Words are no longer enough: we must stop the trafficking that fuels war!”

img.alt: Guardia di Finanza officers seen from inside the cabin of a Global Sumud Flotilla sailboat in Livorno’s harbor on October 22, 2026.

figure.figcaption: Guardia di Finanza officers seen from inside the cabin of a Global Sumud Flotilla sailboat in Livorno’s harbor on October 22, 2026. (Andrea Bellaroto)

div.p: The dockworkers suspended their strike after winning a meeting with Livorno’s Prefecture, TDT, the Port Authority, and the harbor master. USB has said that four “suspicious” containers waiting to be loaded onto Sunaid X held drone batteries, military equipment, gas, and propellants, a claim that has not been independently verified. According to the striking dockworkers, the Port Authority agreed to inspect the cargo, but it is unconfirmed whether the inspection took place or what it found. The Sunaid X has since left for Augusta, in Sicily, where it was again met by GSF activists at sea on Monday.

header.h2: The Latest Action of a Yearlong Effort

div.p: Thursday’s joint GSF-USB-GAP action is the latest in a year of escalating attempts by Livorno’s dockworkers to stop war cargo from moving through their port. It was also the first time GSF boats and striking dockworkers moved together against the same vessel.

“You have to pick the important cases,” said Giovanni Ceraolo, who has organized with USB since 2014 and now works on its national ports coordination. “You have to understand what the right moment is and the right situation, because if you think you can block everything, in the end, you block nothing.”

Ceraolo sat down with me for an hour-long interview, conducted through an interpreter, on October 20, the day the Sunaid X was first due in port. “Weapons pass through the ports every day,” he said, “and it would be practically impossible to think you could block every shipment.”

Livorno’s harbor master’s office reported that more than six hundred tons of explosives, mostly ammunition and rocket motors, were shipped from the port to countries outside the European Union between January 2025 and May 2026, though the data, obtained by the journalist Linda Maggiori and port safety representatives, do not show where any of it ended up.

Law 185 of 1990 bars Italy from exporting arms to countries at war or under embargo and from letting them pass through its ports. The law is “almost never enforced,” Ceraolo said, but he noted that filing a formal complaint, “together with the action, the strike,” has at times been enough to call a shipment into question. Enforcing it has become a standing demand of the port strikes, and it was a plank of the national port strike that USB and ORSA Porti called in May.

Still, Ceraolo was clear that it would not matter if the shipments were judged legal under the law. “Even if there were military traffic authorized under this law, we’d be against it anyway, and we’d act anyway,” he said. “Weapons are weapons, period.”

USB and GAP have developed a three-pronged method, to which GSF has now added a blockade by sea: “Information, pickets, strike. That’s the only method we have for now, and it’s working, on and off.” The information comes mostly from the dockworkers.

When activists blocked a military train at Pisa in March, Ceraolo said, the tip came from workers at the Piombino steelworks, where the train was being loaded. Next, the picket and the strike play out on the ground.

“In practice, there are only two ways to block this traffic: with pickets and blockades, and with the strike. When we’ve managed to do both, we’ve pulled it off.” Put a physical blockade together with a strike in the rail and port sectors that have to handle the cargo, he said, and “you put war logistics in serious difficulty.”

He traces the method back to September 2025. As the fall Global Sumud Flotilla sailed toward Gaza, protesters forced open one of the port’s gates and occupied the quay where the SLNC Severn, a US-flagged ship serving the nearby US Army base at Camp Darby, was due to berth. “We stayed there three days straight, twenty-four hours a day,” Ceraolo said. “All together: students, workers, dockworkers, teachers, the whole city. Even the mayor came.”

The ship never docked. “For us, it was an important event,” he said, because of how close Livorno is to “one of the biggest American bases in Europe.” A week later, the Israeli-owned ZIM Virginia docked and left the same evening without loading or unloading any cargo, after dockworkers struck at the call of Filt-CGIL, the transport federation of Italy’s largest national union confederation.

When Israel intercepted the flotilla in October 2025, Livorno joined the general strike that shut down ports and highways and disrupted rail lines across Italy. Even the organizers were unprepared for the national reverberations of the call to action.

“What happened last year was something nobody in Italy expected, and least of all us in Livorno,” Ceraolo said. “We were flooded with phone calls from people asking how to go on strike, because these were people who had never been on strike in their lives. They didn’t even know what striking meant.” People “who, the day before, never even thought about it were, the next day, behind a burning barricade on the Aurelia,” the coastal highway, he said. “Ordinary people.”

The lesson Ceraolo took was that mass moments can’t be summoned on command. “There’s nothing automatic between daily work and mass moments,” he said. “You have to try, you have to push, talk to people.” What September and October proved, he said, is “that if the conditions are there, people will take to the streets.”

img.alt: Left: a poster for the October 30 general strike on a door in Livorno. Right: Giovanni Ceraolo of the Unione Sindacale di Base (USB). October 20, 2026.

figure.figcaption: Left: a poster for the October 30 general strike on a door in Livorno. Right: Giovanni Ceraolo of the Unione Sindacale di Base (USB). October 20, 2026. (Andrea Bellaroto)

div.p: On October 30, international dockworkers, seafarers, and port workers plan to test that idea well beyond Livorno. The day of action grew out of a declaration agreed on by Mediterranean and European port unions in Istanbul in May. In July, it was announced by unions in six countries: France, Greece, the Basque Country, Turkey, Morocco, and Italy, where USB and ORSA Porti signed on. Organizers now say about one hundred ports in seventeen countries will take part, among them dockworkers in Oakland, Hamburg, and Veracruz, and that around forty thousand containers could be held up for the day. In Italy, eight ports are set to strike, Livorno and Genoa among them, and USB has called a general strike across every sector.

The sectoral demands go beyond the genocide in Gaza. Organizers are calling for an end to using ports to move arms to war zones or as bases for NATO, the US, or EU militaries; an end to European rearmament; and higher wages for the workers who keep the ports running. The strike has been endorsed by seventeen Palestinian trade union bodies.

header.h2: Disturbing the Machine From the Inside

div.p: “I have a son, who is what drives me to do what I do,” said Simone D’Aversa, a thirty-nine-year-old Livorno dockworker who helped found GAP. Over the past few years, he said, he came to see his own work as “extremely involved in war,” and it pushed him to act. “It made me commit: to try to find a way to become something that disturbs this machine from the inside.”

Italy’s labor movement has two tiers. The big national confederations — the Italian General Confederation of Labor (CGIL), the Italian Confederation of Trades Unions (CISL), and the Italian Labour Union (UIL), known in Italian as the confederali — negotiate the national contracts that set most workers’ pay. Smaller, independent sindacati di base, or rank-and-file unions such as USB, have built their membership on the shop floor. When GAP started out, D’Aversa said, the group went to every union in the port and asked them to protect any worker who refused to handle certain cargo.

“On one side, we found USB willing,” he said. “It’s a rank-and-file union that had already been working against the arms trade for years. On the other side, we hit a wall” with the union confederations.

GAP’s members now range from USB members to workers without a union. Some still belong to the big unions, he said, and these workers are unhappy with them but can’t break away “for reasons that are also purely about their jobs.” He described GAP and USB as two “gears” that are “separate and autonomous from each other. In practice, when it’s needed for blockades and strikes, they act as a single entity.”

The organized dockworkers can’t do it alone, D’Aversa said. GAP works with what he called “a strong city network” of student collectives, social centers, associations, and environmental groups. “There’s a real diversity of struggles, and that’s partly what lets us make up for the fact that, yes, we represent Livorno’s dockworkers, but not all of Livorno’s dockworkers,” he said. “So we need a push that also comes from the territory and from the city, which is starting to feel that the port [is] something collective.” He sees that push as an expression of larger possibilities. In Italy, he said, there is “a total lack of trust in politics, in institutional politics, and instead a huge need among people to feel part of politics.”

img.alt: Left: cranes at the Port of Livorno. Right: Simone D’Aversa, a Livorno dockworker who helped found the Gruppo Autonomo Portuali. October 20, 2026.

figure.figcaption: Left: cranes at the Port of Livorno. Right: Simone D’Aversa, a Livorno dockworker who helped found the Gruppo Autonomo Portuali. October 20, 2026. (Andrea Bellaroto)

div.p: Last fall’s mobilizations, he said, “came from a union’s leadership, yes, but just as much from the push the masses gave [for] the union to move.” What gave that push a direction was a speech in Genoa by Riccardo Rudino of CALP, Genoa’s autonomous dockworkers’ collective, who promised that, if the flotilla was stopped, the ports would block everything. “Having a date and a clear goal was the spark that made all the mobilizations possible.”

“It’s true that governments are complicit in what happened,” D’Aversa said. “But I think the act that most challenges our privilege is admitting that we are complicit with our governments, if we don’t do [on October 30] what we did in September and October.”

For Luca Poggi, a twenty-nine-year-old former economist at an environmental nongovernmental organization (NGO), who quit his job after the flotilla’s second mission to organize full-time with GSF, the boats are the seafaring half of the same confrontation at the port. “The disruption of the supply chain is what can hit the genocide the most,” he said, “because you hit on the economics.” The people GSF is up against, he said, “are CEOs of big banks, big investment funds . . . prime ministers of important governments. So, we are fighting against the most powerful people and the most powerful entities in the world.”

GSF, he stressed, does not break the supply chain itself. “We don’t go and assault vessels. We are nonviolent.” He emphasized that the point is numbers. “They might be a hundred. We will be one million,” he said. “The moment we are one million, even money loses its value.” The boats have become a symbol of “David against Goliath . . . we load toys, baby formula, food, medicines, and we go against those who load bullets.” The sea gives GSF room to maneuver that acting on land does not. “It’s much easier to act at sea than acting on land,” he said. “The sea doesn’t have the same law of the land.”

img.alt: Luca Poggi of the Global Sumud Flotilla aboard a sailboat in Livorno’s harbor, with a handheld radio. October 20, 2026.

figure.figcaption: Luca Poggi of the Global Sumud Flotilla aboard a sailboat in Livorno’s harbor, with a handheld radio. October 20, 2026. (Andrea Bellaroto)

div.p: Two days before Thursday’s blockade, Poggi called it GSF’s “way to launch the strike of the 30th of October, Flotilla-style.” The goal was to “show the participation of this company in the war and in the genocide, and also the complicity of our governments that allow all this to happen.” Each sailboat would take a role at a different stage of the ship’s maneuvering, and planning for the action was conducted in person on the boats while awaiting the arrival of Sunaid X.

“Consider that the ship we want to block is eight thousand tons, while our boats are less than eight,” he said. “We will not do anything dangerous. We will stay far. But at the same time, we have ways to block it from entering the port.”

“If a ship is delayed by one day, the delays pile up, and a logistics mechanism breaks,” Ceraolo said. “It’s a political signal but also economic damage. Both things together. So, for us, beyond everything, it’s a historic day.”

entry.title: Election Denial Is Now Normal for the Right Everywhere

div.p: The series of recent elections across the globe have been read as a stinging defeat for right-wing authoritarians, which they are. But maybe more notable is another element: that denial of and efforts to simply reverse unfavorable election results now seem to have become de rigueur for the transnational Right.

All four of the major elections taking place in the ten-day period from October 25 to November 3 have seen or are seeing efforts by right-wing politicians to cast doubt on results where they lost or are likely to, and to engineer a way to change them in their favor.

In Brazil, right-wing candidate Flávio Bolsonaro — whose father is serving a twenty-seven-year prison sentence for trying to organize a coup when he lost the presidential election four years ago — responded to his own shock defeat by announcing a legal challenge to annul the result over the courts’ last-minute extension of voting hours (even though his own campaign had requested the extension). Flávio has now, Juan Guaidó–style, just declared himself the president from Miami, alleging election fraud (before, confusingly, almost immediately deleting the post and declaring himself the country’s rightful “leader” instead).

In Serbia, where the authoritarian former President Aleksandar Vučić was toppled from power after twelve years, there were mounting signs he was preparing to launch a violent coup after badly losing the election, before changing his mind and conceding. By the account of one of Serbia’s own former top anti-terrorism officials, Vučić had “sent 4,000 police and 3,000 thugs to central Belgrade” but was talked down from going through with it by European officials.

In Israel, the scandal-tainted and genocidal Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has now engineered an investigation by Shin Bet, the country’s domestic security service, into the unprecedented voter share won by Israel’s Arab parties, having accused them of “stealing” the election. If Netanyahu’s opposition can get over their refusal to form a government with Arabs, they will block Netanyahu from another stint as prime minister.

And of course, there’s the originator himself: US President Donald Trump, who has since virtually the moment he entered office last year been carrying out a slow-rolling, telegraphed effort to delegitimize the upcoming midterm election result, as presidents’ parties tend to suffer a setback in midterms. As part of this effort, Trump and, at this point, pretty much the entire Republican Party have incessantly seeded the idea that election results can’t be trusted and that his opponents will “cheat” (even as he’s publicly urged his own voters to “cheat like hell”), and they have done everything from trying to purge voters and preemptively challenging the legitimacy of the Alaska election to reportedly discussing simply refusing to certify election results.

Six years ago, Trump’s claims that his 2020 election loss was rigged and efforts to overturn it were read as just the irresponsible sour grapes of one particularly dishonest, erratic politician. (Though let’s give credit where credit’s due: he was technically beaten to the punch in recent years by fellow losers in Indonesia, Ecuador, and especially Bolivia, where in 2019 Trump’s first administration backed the Right’s effort to baselessly cast doubt on and ultimately overturn its election loss through a coup.)

But the election-denial movement Trump kick-started and that is now a nationwide phenomenon has become something of a model beyond US borders. This flat-out refusal to accept defeat and simply live in a self-created, alternate reality where the loser has actually won, numbers be damned, has now become standard operating procedure for right-wing leaders.

According to the International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance’s 2024 report on the state of global democracy, losing candidates rejected the result in 20 percent of the world’s elections between 2020 and 2024, something it calls a “growing phenomenon.” That includes Guatemala in 2023, Peru in 2021, and Brazil in 2022. (To be fair, it’s not always right-wingers — Colombia’s leftist former President Gustavo Petro at one point suspended the presidential transition earlier this year, alleging fraud.)

Some of this recent spate of efforts to reverse the democratic process have failed or look doubtful because the victory margin for the winners made them untenable — reportedly the reason why both Bolsonaro and Vučić aborted their nascent attempts to steal the election.

We will have to see how Netanyahu’s effort fares. The historic 80 percent turnout from Arab voters will make it hard to invalidate votes, and multiple reports have it that the alleged foreign interference that supposedly led to it was actually small-scale and “not something that hasn’t happened in the past.” But Netanyahu’s play may be to use this to make it politically impossible for his opposition to form a government with the Arab parties. Trump’s efforts will likewise be concentrated on those states where the result is likely to be close — but those, too, could be undermined if Democratic candidates end up outdoing polling in the face of widespread unhappiness with Trump’s presidency.

Whatever happens, election denial seems firmly here to stay and is now global. We may end up collectively dodging the very worst-case scenarios of election theft this time. But what happens when future results are close enough or otherwise conducive to right-wing claims of illegitimacy and efforts to overturn? It’s a question the Left now, sadly, has to plan and organize for no matter where one happens to live.

entry.title: The US Is Starving Cuba. Will It Invade Too?

div.p: On September 25, CBS News announced that it had obtained “exclusive new information” regarding potential US military action against Cuba. According to an Army Reserve memo reviewed by the network, the Pentagon was looking at the possibility of mobilizing police forces, medical personnel, and other units to support such an operation. Vague on details, the conveniently timed piece appeared suited to coincide with Donald Trump’s speech at the United Nations three days prior, where he asserted that his administration was seeking a “fundamental change in the situation” with the Cuban government, which is “failing like never before” and “will fall.”

The very night of its report, however, CBS published another article effectively walking it back, quoting a defense expert who claimed that the memo in question should be viewed as a routine planning exercise — one with electoral overtones. “It may be aligned with the interest in trying to inspire the South Florida vote to rally around the administration,” said Florida International University’s Brian Fonseca, “and not necessarily fall into the trap of mismanaged expectations.”

Nearly a month later, and with no invasion in sight, the Florida state government waded still further into pre-electoral waters, issuing an arrest warrant against former President Raúl Castro for his purported responsibility in the 1996 downing of two “Brothers to the Rescue” aircraft. Castro was the defense minister at the time. Essentially a copy-paste of a federal indictment unsealed in May, the announcement came some thirty years after the events in question but a mere two weeks before unusually competitive midterm elections, where even some safe GOP seats in Florida, like that of Cuban American hardliner Maria Elvira Salazar, are suddenly at risk.

In this manner, after ten months of excruciating suffering and the will-they-won’t-they threat of invasion, the medieval siege of ten million Cubans becomes yet one more political football in the US election season.

Following the kidnapping of President Nicolás Maduro of Venezuela and his wife, Cilia Flores, on the night of January 3, rhetoric was flying high in Trumpworld that Cuba would be next. “I think they’re in a lot of trouble,” said Marco Rubio on the day following the operation. “Cuba looks like it’s ready to fall,” Trump himself commented on Air Force One the same day. “I don’t know if they’re going to hold out.” A week later on Truth Social, he threatened: “I strongly suggest they make a deal BEFORE IT IS TOO LATE.” Cuban American congressman Carlos Giménez gloated that “Maduro has fallen, [Cuban President Miguel] Díaz-Canel and [Nicaraguan President Daniel] Ortega are next.” Not to be outdone, Senator Lindsey Graham warned: “You just wait for Cuba.” And so on in an orgy of triumphalist bloviation lasting weeks.

The invasion, however, did not come. What came instead was a total fuel blockade of the island, a flagrant violation of United Nations Charter Article 2(4), Resolution 3314 Article 3(c), and the rules governing freedom of navigation and boarding on the high seas. A whirlwind of executive orders and State Department directives followed, tightening the screws even further. (This on top of Trump having returned Cuba to the list of state sponsors of terrorism on his first day back in office, reversing a removal the Biden administration had waited until its final days to make.) The administration declared a “national emergency” regarding Cuba and expanded sanctions, allowing US authorities to freeze the US-held assets of Cuban officials, government-linked entities, and others.

Foreign companies and banks now face sanctions for doing business with designated parties, and military-linked firms such as the conglomerate Grupo de Administración Empresarial S.A. (GAESA) are walled off entirely: even indirect transactions with entities on the Cuba Restricted List are banned. Foreigners working in key sectors like energy, defense, mining, financial services, or security have been threatened with sanctions. Travel rules for US citizens were also tightened, as were visa rules for Cuban officials and anyone tied to the country’s overseas medical and labor programs. Remittances and money transfers were restricted further. And beyond the specific rules, the measures created a climate of legal uncertainty about penalties and compliance costs that scares off commercial activity of every kind, which was very convenient for Washington.

The result of this avalanche of coercion has, predictably, been devastating. Hotels and resorts such as Spain’s Meliá and Iberostar, Canada’s Blue Diamond, Indonesia’s Archipelago International, and Thailand’s Minor announced they were suspending service on the island. Visa and Mastercard ceased operations in June. Faltering demand and fuel shortages led major airlines like Iberia to cancel direct flights. Shippers such as France’s CMA CGM and Germany’s Hapag-Lloyd suspended new bookings. Over forty banks have ceased operating. A crisis, in short, that may have broken many populations on its own; but not the Cubans, inured like few to withstanding hardship.

“Never before has a sequence of measures been set in motion in such a short period of time that so cold-bloodedly carries out a criminal design of extermination — a policy deliberately aimed at creating shortages capable of suffocating a population, threatening its physical well-being, and depriving an entire people of their means of subsistence,” said Ambassador Johana Tablada de la Torre, deputy chief of mission at the Cuban embassy in Mexico, in an interview.

Tablada de la Torre lays out just some of the results of the blockade: the infant mortality rate in Cuba, once the pride of the nation and the best in the Western Hemisphere, has more than doubled to 9.9 per 1,000. Survival for childhood cancer has tumbled twenty points to 65 percent. Some 96,000 people are on a waitlist for operations, 11,000 of them children.

“The United States is applying the same formula to Cuba that it applied to Gaza, only without the bombs yet,” she says. “And we can’t rule that out. Their theory is that the blockade wasn’t working because it wasn’t airtight. So if they make it airtight and cut off every source of support, the country has to collapse. The opposite is true: it is thanks to our socialist system that we’ve been able to distribute the little we have.” Tablada de la Torre continues:

blockquote.p: The idea is to intervene, install a puppet government, and restore the colonial rule that existed before. They’ve succeeded in the first respect . . . in making the Cuban people suffer like never before in their history. The only thing comparable was the reconcentration period under [General] Valeriano Weyler, during Spanish rule, when the people were confined to camps. . . . so they could not support the rebels. That’s the only comparison. But where they have not succeeded is in their main objective. They have failed to bring the Cuban people to their knees, because they have not managed to force them to give up their struggle.

div.p: Despite the drastic shortages, life goes on in Havana and elsewhere on the island. The bakers bake; the teachers teach; the doctors treat with what they have, while the scientists in the labs move forward as they can. On the streets, the whir of electric vehicles has replaced the grind and groan of the internal combustion engine. As hours of electricity are both precious and unpredictable, people have taken to leaving a small appliance on in order to be woken up if the power comes back on in the middle of the night.

To boost electricity production, the government is banking on two main solutions: First, a China-powered solar revolution that is already producing one gigawatt of the three the country needs to function during peak-demand hours. And second, a developing technology called “thermoconversion” capable of improving the quality of the heavy crude oil found on its north coast by reducing its viscosity and sulfur content. Unsurprisingly, the attempt at energy sovereignty has also become a target of Trumpian sabotage, with the Center for Petroleum Investigation (CEINPET) being included in the July round of sanctions, almost three months after the announcement of the breakthrough.

So where does all of this leave the prospect of an invasion? In short, in a very strange space. In the months since the setting up of the oil blockade, Western media has been on a febrile search for the “perfect traitor” that would hand over the keys to the island and defuse popular resistance. For a time over the summer, on the heels of CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s visit to the island, they even thought they’d found one in the person of Raúl Guillermo Rodríguez Castro, Raúl Castro’s grandson and Fidel’s grandnephew.

It was not to be. By October, Marco Rubio was forced to take to X to effectively crowdsource an uprising, calling on “those who seek to create positive change in Cuba” to seize the opportunity “through a discrete [sic] partnership with the CIA.” Not very discreetly, the CIA then took it upon itself to retweet Rubio, translating the text into Spanish, only for the US Southern Command to then retweet the CIA. To cap off the delirium, Donald Trump insisted at a campaign stop on October 23 that “we’ll take care of Cuba on our way back from Iran,” conjuring up the unlikely image of a warship stopping fifty yards off the coast only for the island’s public to spontaneously raise up its hands in surrender. Meanwhile, polls consistently show the US public opposing an invasion by overwhelming margins.

As for the “taking care of Cuba” on the way back from Iran, there are two schools of thought. The first is that the Trumpian debacle in West Asia makes an invasion of Cuba less likely, as it stands to suck up attention, resources, soldiers, and carriers for months or even years to come. The “pink tide” of progressive governments in Latin America, according to this thesis, was at least partially due to the Bush administration’s being distracted by the occupation of Afghanistan and Iraq. But many in the region hold another view, darker and more fatalistic perhaps, but rooted in history and a long-standing study of US character: that a disaster in Iran could actually make such an attack more likely, as the empire will need a smaller enemy to brutalize in order to staunch its wounded pride. The war in Iran is hardly preventing the Trump administration from intervening in country after country in the region as we speak, these people would argue. Although an extended occupation, which is what Cuba would most likely require, is another matter entirely.

Despite Trump’s fantasies and the obvious asymmetries involved, a hypothetical invasion would be anything but a walk in the park. “The United States surpasses us in firepower and military technology, but if they lose their minds and make the reckless decision to attack us, the cannons will roar in Cuba, and many of our people will die — but so will many of theirs,” warns Tablada de la Torre.

entry.title: Is There Life After AI? Cory Doctorow Thinks So.

div.p: The artificial intelligence boom is fueled by an elite wager that software can supplant expensive human expertise. The tech industry and its investors are pumping hundreds of billions of dollars into the technology — Goldman Sachs forecasts that global AI-related investment will soon exceed $1 trillion. At the same time, government regulatory regimes are inadequate and consumer use cases often vague, misleading, or utterly counterproductive.

The economics of AI don’t make sense unless one factors in what its backers hope to gain: a way to displace workers. In his most recent book, The Reverse Centaur’s Guide to Life After AI, Cory Doctorow explains how people have become tools of the machines and the capitalists who own them.

Doctorow recently spoke to Jacobin to discuss the rise of AI, the financial conjuring tricks behind the boom, the copyright fight, what it all means for workers — and why the answer to AI doomerism lies in building workers’ rights and public power.

dt.p: David Moscrop

People talk about AI all the time. You get through the conversation and realize no one has specified what they’re talking about. So, I want to start with the simplest, most complicated question. What is AI?

dd.p: Cory Doctorow

That question implies that you understand the most important thing about AI, which is that we call something different “AI” every five to ten years, and we’ve been doing that since the mid-1950s. You could say AI is the label we apply to anything that is doing something that we currently believe is the unique province of a conscious mind. Then it stops being AI once we realize that it’s doing that without being a conscious mind, and we apply the label to something else.

But this new, specific kind of AI is actually really useful and interesting from a class-struggle perspective. It’s useful to understand what this AI does differently from the AIs that preceded it. Before this version of AI, we had something we called symbolic AI. The way it worked was that you’d build a software model of the thing that you wanted to use machine learning on. If you wanted to use machine learning to figure out how to play chess, you would first build a software model of a chess board, chess pieces, and chess rules. Then you would use machine learning — a statistical technique that involves analyzing previous games, running iterations, and asking for human feedback — to try to improve the chess game that the AI could play.

What the current version of AI does, this theory-free version, is it swaps out these models of the world for a brute-force approach. This is why we call it theory-free. We take all the stuff in the world we can observe, and we feed it to all the computers we can find, and we ask the computers to find statistical relationships between things to try to understand whether A causes B. And while we all know correlation is not causation, causes and effects are correlated.

The problem of correlation and causation is that you might think A causes B, but actually it’s A and A’ that cause B. But A and A’ happen at the same time 99.9999 percent of the time, so we can’t distinguish between them. The answer with AI is to keep adding training data until there are enough examples, even with a thing that only happens one in a million times, that we can actually see that it’s A and A’ that’s causing B and not just A. And we just keep throwing more computing power at it.

The weird thing is that we do this for things where we actually know how they work. We know how to play chess, but we ask LLMs to play chess for us. The problem is that, because they’re theory-free, they don’t know what a chess board is. If you ask an LLM to play chess, it will sometimes put a piece on a square where it already has a piece because it doesn’t know that it’s playing chess. It’s just pulling statistical guesses out of a multidimensional array that tries to represent the relationship of every chess move to every other chess move in the training set. So that’s what is going on here.

We’re also using it to try and pull out statistical relationships between things whose causality we don’t understand. There are far more things in the world that we don’t understand than those we do, but we can observe what seems like a causal relationship.

If you get sick tonight and go to the doctor, you might get a medicine whose method of action is not understood. But we know it works, so we give it to people who are sick. We don’t always wait until we understand it before using it — although we do study it.

But here’s the thing: by building a system where we can swap brute force for understanding — so, money for theory — we clear the very last hurdle for finance capital as a source of power. Expertise and money are both unevenly distributed, but money is collected in the hands of people who don’t have much expertise, while expertise is collected in the hands of people who don’t have much money.

There is a durable source of power among experts. If you don’t want to work for Arthur Sackler, he can’t make you. And if you’re the only person who understands some abstruse area of pharmacology, Arthur Sackler can’t do research in that area. But Arthur Sackler is very, very rich. When you swap expertise for money, you don’t need to convince the only pharmacologist who understands some narrow area to come work for you. You can just throw money at the problem.

This is why the AI industry raised a trillion dollars this year on $50 billion revenue: because the finance sector is in love with the idea of a technology where money can be substituted for expertise.

header.h2: The Brief Life of the Big-Firm Wage Premium

dt.p: David Moscrop

In your latest book, you describe this dynamic as a reverse centaur — “a machine that uses a human being as its assistant” instead of the other way around. How did we end up on the other half of this thing? Can we flip it back around?

dd.p: Cory Doctorow

That dynamic is intrinsic to this kind of AI, in the sense that this kind of AI is really, really expensive and only starts to make money if you can displace a lot of high-wage labor. And this is another area where we have to be really careful to be good materialists and distinguish the sizzle from the steak. Pauperizing commercial artists, pornography performers, and taxi drivers is not a way to recoup the expense associated with training AI. These companies are not doing this to get rich. They’re doing it to demonstrate how awesomely powerful the AI is.

No language on earth contains the phrase “as rich as a taxi driver.” Replacing Uber drivers who supply the cars, insurance, depreciation, fuel, and the cost of shampooing vomit out of the backseat with expensive robots that you own doesn’t pencil out — unless your goal is to say, “If we can replace taxi drivers, imagine what we can do to accountants, lawyers, doctors, teachers, radiologists, nurses. And especially people who work in fields where you are legally obliged to tell your boss to f-ck off if they tell you to commit a crime, like medicine, finance, education, and so on.”

That’s what has them so excited. We got here because they saw an opportunity — in both the narrative around AI and the surprising statistical smoothness of reality that AI revealed — to both scare workers into docility and, in some cases, to replace workers with software. If you can do both, the software doesn’t have to be capable of doing the worker’s job, because you can acquire enough market power to produce inferior outputs that the public is still required to consume. That’s the goal of every monopolist: to raise prices and lower quality, which you can only do if you have market power.

This is why competition matters more than a lot of leftists think it does. It disciplines firms because they have to worry about competitors. And the presence of competitors makes it more difficult for firms to solve the collective action problem needed to capture a regulator and to capture a workforce.

I think some leftists believe that the short-lived and extremely contingent large-firm wage premium, where very large firms with a lot of market share paid their workers more out of the excess profits they generated, was a state of nature, and that we need to go back to having really big companies with enough profit to share with us. That’s not true. That was a highly contingent moment in which the hangover from the New Deal coincided with the first days of monopoly — the post–New Deal monopoly surge.

There was enough labor power left to force monopolists to part with some of their ill-gotten booty. But that was never going to be a durable condition, because they were going to accelerate their market power, and that would necessarily dampen labor power. That’s what competition is good for: not as an end unto itself but as a way to shatter the class solidarity of the ruling class.

dt.p: David Moscrop
Is the industry in a bubble? You see headlines like “Stock Market Had Its Best Ever Year.” I look at headlines from 1929 and think, I’m not convinced that’s such a good omen.

dd.p: Cory Doctorow

It is a bubble. I’m not questioning that it’s a bubble. I’m trying to find the ideological and material roots of the bubble. And as a good materialist, I think ideology is downstream of material conditions.

Billionaires don’t like to be thwarted. We can think of billionaire-ism as the pathological state of being angry about being thwarted. We all get called on our bullsh-t from time to time, and sometimes that’s bad because it’s not bullsh-t. But a lot of the time, actually we were wrong, and it’s good that someone was around to call us on our bullsh-t. This is why married people live longer — because there’s someone who can say “No, you’ve got to go to the doctor. No, you have to go and you have to stop eating that.” Being called on your own bullsh-t is good, but billionaires are in a pathological condition of not wanting to be called on theirs.

I also think there’s this other material story about the bubble. Growth stocks have much higher valuations than mature stocks, not because of superstition or a commitment to growth, but because a share is a claim on future earnings. Growing companies have more future earnings than stable ones. Highly valued stocks are also highly liquid, and so they can be used as a substitute for cash. If you want to grow by hiring people or buying other companies, you can use shares to do that if your company’s stock is highly liquid — which is to say, if it’s growing.

Shares are really nice from a firm’s perspective because you can make them endogenously by typing zeros into a spreadsheet, whereas money is something you don’t get to make endogenously without being arrested. You have to get it from banks or investors or creditors or customers. So, firms don’t want to reach the point where markets view them as mature, because they lose that special advantage, and they also lose a ton of their valuation. If you cease to be a growth company, your valuation should have an earnings multiple commensurate with that of a mature company, which is something like 10 percent of the price-to-earnings ratio of a growth company. That means that you become 90 percent poorer the day the market decides you’re not growing anymore.

And I know we say, “Oh, endless growth is the ideology of a tumor,” but it’s not ideological to not want to be 90 percent poorer. That is a purely material phenomenon. On the one hand, you have a narrative need to tell a story about how a company that has undeniably saturated its market — Google has a 90 percent search market share; it has saturated the market — is going to grow into some adjacent sector. It could be one that we can all point to and agree exists like, “Oh, we’re doing Google Plus, so we’re about to become Facebook.” Or it might be a fanciful one that you have to convince people might exist, like Web3, cryptocurrency, the Metaverse, or whatever. But on the other hand, because it doesn’t exist, you can make extremely fanciful claims about its eventual valuation. You’re the expert on it because you just invented it.
And so you have Morgan Stanley saying, “Mark Zuckerberg’s right. The Metaverse is an $8 trillion play.”

dt.p: David Moscrop
Reminds me of NFTs [non-fungible tokens].

dd.p: Cory Doctorow

NFTs, yeah, which were DOA. AI comes in as the latest version of this. The question isn’t “Is there an AI bubble?” There’s an AI bubble for the same reason that there was a cryptocurrency bubble. The question is “Why is the AI bubble so much bigger?”

On the one hand, it’s so much bigger because the computer science is more real. We should not underestimate how surprising it is to discover the degree of statistical regularity in the universe with this theory-free AI. The fact that you can have a thing that closely resembles a conversation with a thinking person just by guessing words is legitimately remarkable. But it doesn’t tell us anything about consciousness — or, at least, that’s not what I think it’s telling us. What I think it’s telling us is that there’s more statistical regularity than our brains would guess without an instrument, in the same way that our brains guess wrong about all kinds of things.

Your brain guesses how long you’ve been waiting in line: “I’ve been here for an hour.” Then you look at your watch, and it’s only been ten minutes. We persistently underestimate how regular things are, and the only way we can discover that is by having this thing that ingests a lot of data and then makes guesses. It’s cool; it’s interesting. I think philosophy departments can dine out on this for the next fifty years. But it wasn’t worth a trillion dollars. So, that’s part of the reason the bubble is so much bigger: the computer science is real, and it discovered an interesting fact about the universe in a way that none of that other stuff did.

Blockchains are also real; they’re just not as interesting. The number of applications for that kind of slow database rounds to zero. It’s money laundering, gambling, ransomware. That’s sort of it. It’s just not all that valuable, whereas this AI stuff is much more interesting.

But the other piece is the ideological one that I alluded to at the beginning: billionaires are very excited about the idea of a means of swapping money for expertise. I think that’s because being a billionaire also means being a solipsist. You can’t make a billion dollars and hurt people in the way that you must in order to make a billion dollars if you think other people experience hurt the way you do. To aspire to a world in which 99.999 percent of the world receives no moral consideration is to aspire to solipsism. AI is a very solipsistic technology. It’s a technology that sort of implies that everyone else is just a bot. If everyone else can be replaced by a bot, then in some sense, everyone else is a bot.

dt.p: David Moscrop
Is this version of AI destined to be commodified? AI companies want to rent intelligence back to us by the meter, using content we’ve created. Does data necessarily become a commodity?

dd.p: Cory Doctorow

The problem is, I think neither of those things are going to work. Selling intelligence as a service requires that the AI companies remain in business. They’re spending a trillion dollars to make $50 billion. Their unit economics just suck.

So, let’s take a little detour into just how sh-tty a business AI is. They’re spending a lot of money to make a little money. That’s not unusual. You spend a lot of money and make a railroad, then make it up by operating the rail carriages over the rails. But there’s a lot of problems with this analogy. In the case of AI, the unit economics — the cost of running the rail carriages over the rails — suck. They lose money on every rail carriage. Every customer they acquire makes them poorer. Every time that customer comes back to use their product, it makes them poorer again.

Every version of AI, every new improvement in AI, loses more money than the previous one. And the depreciation schedule sucks. They’ll tell you that they need to upgrade the hardware every five years. They’re actually upgrading it every two to three years, which is wild, because that’s just accounting fraud. If you’ve got assets on your book that you are treating internally as though they’re worthless, but you’re telling the market and your investors that there’s still 40 percent of their value left, then calling that accounting fraud is doing violence to accounting fraud. It’s just terrible.

And it matters because even five years of $50 billion in annual revenue wouldn’t be enough to recoup a trillion-dollar investment. But their unit economics are not improving. They keep claiming they’re improving. They keep saying, “Well, the cost of inference” — which is the operating expense — “is going down.” It’s not.

dt.p: David Moscrop
How does the inference model work?

dd.p: Cory Doctorow

So, you have training and you have inference. Training is when you ingest all the data, and you find its statistical relations. Inference is like when some chud goes to Grok and says, “Make me Sonic the Hedgehog, but with giant tits.” They keep saying inference is getting cheaper, but it’s not. And when you look at the balance sheets, you discover that they’re doing the world’s sweatiest tricks to hide this fact.

Ed Zitron is quite a good and attentive and detail-oriented watcher of AI. Someone leaked him a copy of OpenAI’s balance sheet, and I can’t think of anyone better to leak to because this is the guy who’s going to go over it as closely as you can imagine, with absolute obsessive detail. He reports that the inference line is a small sum of money. But he also reports that if you keep running your finger down the balance sheet, you get to the marketing budget and find that OpenAI claims to spend more on marketing than Coca-Cola.

Coca-Cola has three global marketing agencies with offices in every major city and billboards on every corner. If you want to know whether Coke is really spending money on marketing, you can verify it just by counting billboards on corners and noses in offices. But there is no evidence that OpenAI is spending that kind of money on marketing. Ed’s thesis, which I think is completely true, is that they’re just calling the inference they give away a marketing expense. But that doesn’t make it not an inference expense. That’s like saying “Oh, it’s not a bald spot. It’s a solar panel for a sex machine.” It’s still a bald spot.

These companies don’t have a way to rightsize their balance sheet. And even if they did — and this is where commodification comes in — the switching costs are really, really low. When Anthropic started overtaking OpenAI, everyone just went to ChatGPT and said, “Package up all of my data in a format that’s easy for Claude to understand.” And then, they deleted their OpenAI accounts, opened Claude accounts, and started paying there.

It’s like if you finish building the Canadian Pacific Railway and turn around, and someone has just put down another set of tracks next to your tracks and their trains are 20 percent faster, and you haven’t run a single goddamn carriage over your tracks yet. So, you’ve got to start building your own set of tracks again.

And this is where the open-source, open-weight models come in. The Chinese are taking low-end hardware and open models, and they’re doing something called distillation. That’s when you methodically query Claude and ChatGPT, then use the answers to train your own model without doing the original training. They can’t stop that.

The idea that they’re going to be able to charge rent forever on inference requires, for example, that they cook up a giant scare about how their word-guessing program is about to become God and kill us all because their hacker bot escaped containment. Then they get the US federal government, on the one hand, to make it legal for them to all agree to stop doing R&D — which would otherwise be a flaming antitrust violation — and on the other, to ban all the Chinese models. Right on schedule, they’ve done that. But it’s not going to work.

dt.p: David Moscrop
What about the copyright-maximalist response to LLMs training on what we create? Does that further commodify intellectual and creative output?

dd.p: Cory Doctorow

First of all, the value of your data for training rounds to zero. All we’re doing is creating a crazy version of markets in which affluent people can afford to keep their data out of the model, while poor people accept a pittance — far less than it’s going to hurt them to have their data in the model — and then that data is used in ways that harm them.

The problem with copyright is that it’s not a labor right. Artists are told that it’s their primary mechanism for defending their labor rights, but it’s a property right. They call it intellectual property. Think about it: property rights are fully alienable. If you’re bargaining into a market of five publishers, and four studios, and three labels, and two app companies, and one company that does the ebooks and audiobooks, having more rights just means you have more to bargain away for the same price.

Copyright has expanded for fifty years. Copyright payments have not. The copyrights required as a matter of boilerplate contract by this highly concentrated monopsony that we sell our creative labor to are just 100 percent of all the rights we’ve ever been given. And every time we get a new right, the standard deal expands.

The Hollywood writers were not on strike against Anthropic and OpenAI. They were on strike against the studio bosses, who want to replace Hollywood writers with AI and who are also suing AI companies over copyright. If they win that right, you can kiss goodbye to the socially productive activities that we do that resemble AI training. If you can’t scrape the web anymore, you can’t make a record of what CBS looked like before Bari Weiss took over.

If you can’t publish factual assertions, you can’t publish factual assertions gathered from large corpuses — like how chuddy CBS is now that Bari Weiss is running it, what racial slurs they’re using, how many articles are being written by people of color, or whatever you want to name. That all goes out the window if we create an exclusive right to make transient copies of works for the purpose of analysis, perform analysis on them, and then to publish the results. Copyright does not currently restrict those activities to block AI training; you would have to make them restricted by copyright.

Then bosses in the extremely concentrated creative labor markets would just acquire those rights as a nonnegotiable condition of employment. They would use them to train chatbots and then fire your -ss and replace you with those sh-tty chatbots that hallucinate because they’re just doing statistical extrapolation.

We would then have inferior outputs, worse wages, and a political environment in which it is even harder to hold rich and powerful people to account. If we build out labor rights, privacy rights, human rights, and consumer rights, which are the good rights, and relegate property rights to where they belong — to those things that are so worthless that we can put a price tag on them — then we actually have a chance against AI.

entry.title: Serbia’s Students Changed How Serbians Think About Politics

div.p: On Sunday, the largest and most sustained student movement in Europe reached its culmination. After two years of protesting and organizing, this fall Serbia’s students mounted an electoral challenge to former President Aleksandar Vučić, who was this time running to become prime minister. His plans were foiled, as the Student List won with over half of all votes, ending fourteen years of rule by Vučić’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS).

With the Serbian election process traditionally marked by irregularities, vote buying, pressure on public workers to vote for the ruling party, one-sided media coverage, and other efforts to manipulate the results, the students faced an enormous task. It was far from clear whether Vučić would concede and accept his defeat in case the students won. The tensions were high throughout voting day, and especially toward the evening, when the reports spread that the center of capital Belgrade was becoming filled with police, riot control vehicles, and pro-government thugs.

A deciding factor was the voter turnout, which reached 69 percent, up from 58.7 percent in 2023. Such a high turnout recalled the historic elections of September 2000 when Slobodan Milošević, an ultranationalist dictator responsible for many of the war crimes of the 1990s, was finally defeated. On Sunday, people lined up for hours at polling stations across Serbia and around the world, where the diaspora also participated. Many of the polling stations had people waiting from 5 or 6 a.m., before they opened. The student movement was also successful in mobilizing election observers who covered almost all of the polling stations, making any effort to manipulate the results much harder.

After the polling stations closed at 8 p.m., Aleksandar Vučić addressed the nation around ninety minutes later. “It is clear that we lost these elections. The student-blockader list won. They will have between 135 and 140 members of parliament, we have around 105,” he announced. Although Vučić still used the pejorative description of the Student List candidates as “blockaders” in his speech as he had throughout his campaign, his relatively quick acceptance of defeat came as a surprise. The Student List achieved an overwhelming victory, winning an absolute majority of 52.65 percent compared to 39.2 percent for Vučić’s SNS.

Such a victory offers inspiration to other student movements across Europe and the world. The Serbian student movement became a unique political force in three important ways — building a collective and “leaderless” power, recentering science, expertise, and institutions, and rebuilding trust in democracy, notably through the emphasis on the principles of direct democracy and collective decision-making.

The student movement emerged after the collapse of a concrete roof canopy of a newly renovated railway station in Novi Sad, the second-largest city, on November 1, 2024, which resulted in the death of sixteen people. Rather than being seen as a tragic incident, the event was immediately interpreted by many Serbian citizens as a result of years of state capture, nepotism, and corruption. Vigils and protests spread across the country, and students of the Faculty of Dramatic Arts in Belgrade decided to occupy the faculty building. The student revolt spread like wildfire, and within days, every university and every faculty in the country was occupied by the students. Over the months, its resistance attracted hundreds of thousands of supporters who gathered at the student-organized protests and marches across the country, offering support, donations, food, and accommodation for the students.

At the occupied faculties, the students organized themselves into so-called plenums — a form of assembly through which decisions were made based on the principles of direct democracy. At plenums, students have been deciding on questions connected to organizing and protests, with every student being able to raise an issue, which is then discussed and voted on. As a result, there is significantly less hierarchy in the decision-making, only (often-rotated) moderators of plenums, and working groups through which tasks are handled, such as working groups on communication with the media and the public, social networks, security at the protests, and the like. Crucially, the principles of direct democracy have spread outside of the blocked faculties, as the students called on the general public in March 2025 to also organize in citizen assemblies called zbors.

Over time, the political demands of the protest movement, centered on investigating the collapse of the Novi Sad train station and holding those in power responsible, transformed into a political program that offered a new vision for the country. Through plenums and collective deliberation and decision-making, the student movement introduced the political program as well as the list of the candidates who were to run in the elections, formed in a process that lasted more than a year. The result was a “leaderless” political force that rejected a cult of personality as a source of power, regardless of the ideology. Just as the student movement has been centered on the collective and rejected any single leader who could be targeted by authorities, the election campaign emphasized collective effort rather than any single person. An antidote to the leadership of strongmen and the concentration of power in the hands of a single person, it became a collective movement that altogether rejected the premises behind representative democracy based on a few charismatic individuals.
As the student movement wrote in its statement introducing the list of 250 candidates:

blockquote.p: The candidates were not chosen by party leaders, nor did anyone compile a list in a room and announce it to the rest. Instead, they were selected by students through a decision-making process we built over almost two years of blockades, plenums, discussions, and collaborative work. That process was neither quick nor simple. Direct democracy rarely is. It entails dialogue, disagreement, argumentation, revisiting decisions, and accountability toward the people participating in the process. That is precisely why it was important to us that we form the electoral list in this way. If we say we want a different political system, it makes no sense that our first step toward that goal is replicating the very model we are fighting against.

div.p: The student movement refused from the beginning to work with the opposition parties and with anyone who had prior experience in Serbian politics, arguing for a completely new beginning. A crucial aspect of the program is trust in experts to run public institutions rather than political appointees. As the students put it in the program, they will seek to “abolish political patronage” and “appoint proven experts rather than party loyalists to head public enterprises.” While many of the Western societies have seen in the past several years an organized erosion of public trust in science and expertise, notably with Donald Trump’s attack on climate science and COVID-19 conspiracies, the student movement has moved in the opposite direction. As a result, more than half of the candidates on the student list have a doctorate. Many are university professors who supported the students during their blockades; others are doctors, engineers, or lawyers; but the list also includes journalists, actors, and artists, as well as farmers and agricultural workers — all experts in their areas. Yet there were no students or opposition politicians. The student movement ran a campaign focused on anti-corruption and pro-democratic efforts, as well as rebuilding the institutions, which ultimately led to their victory.

Vučić’s rule was marked by strong control of the media landscape and by the oppression of those who opposed him, from police violence to targeting students, journalists, and activists with Israeli spyware technology on their phones. Yet the student movement did not overthrow an isolated dictator, but a leader who was a strategic partner for a range of geopolitical actors. Vučić’s authoritarian regime has proven useful for the European Union and China alike, Serbia’s largest trading partners and foreign direct investors, but also to the United States, Russia, Israel, and many others. During his time in power, Vučić strengthened Serbia’s ties to Russia as well as to Donald Trump and his family, and he ramped up arms exports to Israel in the past three years — which have increased by forty-two times since 2023, when Israel began its genocidal campaign in Gaza.

As for the EU, one of its key interests in Serbia has been a large deposit of lithium, the mining of which, however, attracted widespread resistance due to the potential environmental impact of the mine planned by an Anglo-Australian mining corporation, Rio Tinto. In 2024, the EU signed a strategic partnership with Serbia on developing the electric vehicle value chain, for which lithium is a key component. In June 2025, during the height of the student protests, the EU chose to ignore countless open letters and petitions, which warned that the support for lithium mining would jeopardize the EU’s image in Serbia, and designated the planned lithium mine as a strategic project under its Critical Raw Materials Act.

The EU’s continuous support for lithium mining despite local concerns for the environment and democratic decision-making is a key reason why relations with the EU played a surprisingly small role in the elections. Unlike at pro-democracy protests in Georgia or Hungary, EU flags were notably missing at the student protests in Serbia. That is also why the student victory should not be necessarily interpreted as a turn toward the EU and the West more generally. Zlatko Kokanović, a farmer who has been at the center of anti-lithium protests and who was a candidate on the Student List, said that he would advocate for a permanent ban on the exploration and exploitation of lithium in Serbia.

Yet the student movement did not emerge from a vacuum. Vučić had faced challenges to his rule and countless protests, from the 2017 protests “Against Dictatorship,” which erupted a day after Vučić won the presidential election, to the aforementioned protests against lithium mining, which spread in 2021 and 2022, attracting tens of thousands of people in protests and blockades and forcing the government to officially cancel the mining project in 2022 (though the cancellation was later nullified, days before the Strategic Partnership with the EU was signed in 2024). Crucially, the different movements were not isolated from one another but cooperated in many ways, with the anti-lithium movement and the students converging on the issue of environmental protection. Still, none of the protest movements was able to mobilize as many people as the student movement.

The slogan “Serbia or the Mafia” helped foster the atmosphere of a referendum between two choices: the Student List on one hand and Vučić’s regime on the other. This was further underscored by the fact that most opposition parties decided against running, to avoid watering down the vote for the Student List. The student movement is widely heterogeneous, with diverse ideologies across the Left and the Right coming together, ranging from nationalists to pro-EU liberals, yet united against authoritarian rule. Still, the political program was clearly centered on anti-corruption efforts, media freedom, food sovereignty, health and environmental protection, and supporting workers’ rights, with initiatives including an improvement of health care access in rural areas and amending the Labor Law to increase job security. As one of the candidates of the Student List, Aleksandar Čupić, a professor at the Faculty of Transport, said in an interview, the goal is to “depoliticize institutions and politicize the society. We should all be concerned with politics.”

header.h2: A Night of Celebration and the Day After

div.p: When the student movement organized a final political gathering before the elections on Thursday, October 22, drawing over 150,000 people to Slavija Square in Belgrade, it promised that after years of protests this would be the last time when the citizens would need to gather in such large numbers.

Yet after Aleksandar Vučić conceded on Sunday evening, people flooded the streets, spontaneously gathering in celebration. Slavia was again filled with tens of thousands of people, though this time in euphoric celebration. The atmosphere was electrifying, with cars honking on the roads, people coming out on their balconies, whistling and shouting in joy. Another day of celebration was scheduled for Monday evening.

The morning after the victory, people gathered in Pionirski Park, just across from the parliament, which had been occupied for a year and a half by pro-government thugs who set up their tents there and threatened passersby and supporters of the students. Though the thugs were finally gone, garbage had piled up. The citizens began cleaning the park and fixing the playground while playing music and dancing in celebration — a small example of all the work that lies ahead of the Student List and their supporters yet an important symbol of citizen organizing.

Undoubtedly, victory in the elections is just the beginning. The geopolitical conditions that enabled Vučić’s rule remain in place, just as the structures of global capitalism do. For his part, Vučić is unlikely to retire from political life but will focus on recapturing his power. Within the Student List, ideological differences, which were set aside for the sake of defeating Vučić, might become more visible, especially when it comes to the questions of nationalism, the approach to Kosovo, and foreign policy more broadly.

Still, by winning the elections, the Serbian students demonstrated that no strongman is untouchable, no matter how deeply entrenched in the system and how unfair the conditions are. The tectonic change in how people understand politics and decision-making has already happened, and it is spreading fast. The global challenge to a handful of leaders who deepen inequalities and sow divisions will only continue to rise.

entry.title: The Food Industry Is Rife With Worker Abuse

div.p: Two things in life are certain: everybody eats, and nothing explains capitalism better than food. A new report from the International Panel of Experts on Sustainable Food Systems (IPES-Food) presents a comprehensive analysis of the exploitation inherent in the global food system, and what needs to be done to change it.

More people work in food than any other sector of the global economy, yet the food system can only function through systemic exploitation. Addressing these contradictions gives us a blueprint for not only tackling the worst aspects of food production but a model for taking on the worst of capitalism in general.

Food systems employ more workers than any sector of the global economy. Roughly 1.4 billion people work in food systems — that’s two out of every five working people. Food workers face low pay, wage theft, forced and child labor, human trafficking, insecure work, discrimination, sexual violence, occupational health and safety risks, and exclusion from social protections. Nearly four hundred million food system workers earn below a living wage. Minimum wage protections are often weak or absent for food system workers, with farmworkers consistently ranked among workers most likely to live in poverty.

Food work has the highest rates of informality of any part of the global economy, excluding workers from basic protections and collective bargaining and leaving them highly vulnerable to exploitation and poverty. Ninety percent of farm work, 80 percent of domestic work, 60 percent of accommodation and food service activities, and 60 percent of wholesale and retail workers are informal. Agriculture consistently ranks as one of the most dangerous sectors to work in worldwide, due to exposure to extreme weather conditions, long shifts without breaks, contact with harmful pesticides and chemicals, and an elevated risk of injury and death.

Food and agriculture are also considered among the highest risk sectors for modern slavery, with impoverished, informal, and migrant workers the most susceptible. There are an estimated 2.1 million forced laborers working in agriculture. Agriculture is also the sector responsible for the highest amount of child labor worldwide. More than 83 million children work in agriculture, accounting for 61 percent percent of global child labor.

Migrant workers are essential to today’s food systems yet face some of the highest levels of exploitation. Restrictive immigration policies make workers more vulnerable to abuse and drive down standards for everyone. Migrants are three times more likely to be trapped in forced labor compared to nonmigrant workers globally and are 70 percent more likely to die on the job. They also lose an estimated $31 billion in wage underpayment by employers annually. Women in food work also face systemic inequalities: wage gaps, harassment and violence, a disproportionate burden of care work, and exclusion from decision-making.

None of this is an accident. Today’s food systems are built on keeping labor cheap and profits high. Weak labor protections, poor enforcement, and unequal power leave millions of workers exposed to exploitation. Governments directly enable exploitation through selective regulations that exempt food and farm employers from basic standards on wages, safety, and collective bargaining. Informal, contract, seasonal, self-employed, and family workers are routinely excluded from workers’ rights.

header.h2: Food Work’s Accelerating Race to the Bottom

div.p: The food system is evolving in ways that deepen exploitation. Rising heat, extreme weather, wildfire smoke, and growing pesticide use are making food work increasingly dangerous. US farmworkers are thirty-five times more likely to die from heat stress than other workers. In Africa, 93 percent of workers are exposed to dangerous heat; most work in food systems.

Corporate concentration is driving a race to the bottom, suppressing wages, weakening unions, outsourcing responsibility, and prioritizing shareholder returns over decent work. Industry consolidation directly undermines bargaining rights; larger food firms show significantly higher rates of illegal union interference, including wrongful terminations, refusals to hire, coercion, and retaliation for union activity.

In 2019, nine of the largest US poultry processors settled for over $398 million in a lawsuit alleging a twenty-year conspiracy to depress wages and target vulnerable populations, including migrants and refugees, to keep pay at or below the poverty line. Similar cases have emerged across pork and beef sectors.

Walmart illustrates the full weight of this dynamic. With 90 percent of the US population living within ten miles of a store, the company captures one in every four grocery dollars — more than the next five supermarket chains combined. This has reduced employment exit options and suppressed wages and benefits. Within ten years of a Walmart Supercenter opening in a community, average household income can fall by 6 percent. Walmart employees use $6.2 billion in public assistance to survive, and the company is the largest redeemer of consumer SNAP and WIC dollars.

Digital technologies are also creating new forms of exploitation. Gig-based platform work, automation, algorithmic management, and digital surveillance are isolating workers, intensifying productivity pressures, increasing injuries, and weakening protections for workers. Digital surveillance and algorithmic management also function as tools for wage suppression, pushing into outright wage theft. Digital productivity tracking intensifies workplace pressure and drives injury rates upward. Employees must work harder simply to maintain incomes that remain both inadequate and unpredictable.

header.h2: The Path to a Different Food System

div.p: Despite these entrenched structural pressures, food workers and advocates are organizing. The efforts are scattered, not always coherent, and take different tacks, from deeply pragmatic and reformist to visionary. But a vastly different food system is possible through five strategies.

Worker power must be the priority, and that means strengthening unions, expanding collective bargaining, and building solidarity across movements. Guaranteeing decent work includes enshrining workers’ rights in law, setting enforceable floors for decent work, and investing in labor inspection and enforcement. Reining in corporate power means holding firms accountable for labor abuses throughout food supply chains. Demanding equal rights for migrant workers includes ending legal exclusions for migrant workers and the criminalization of migrants. Valuing food work means recognizing, protecting, and rewarding the skills, knowledge, and care of the people who feed us. These are the formulas that social movements are applying throughout the world.

In India, street vendors are organized under the National Hawkers Federation, an association of over 1,650 unions across twenty-eight states. In the United States, farmworker-led models initiated by the Coalition of Immokalee Workers are utilizing legally binding agreements to ensure suppliers respect workers’ rights and provide higher wages. Workers set their own labor standards and oversee independent investigation and enforcement systems funded by the companies themselves.

Public sector supply chains in Brazil and the United States are enacting purchasing requirements that protect supply chain workers and ensure more sustainable and diversified growers and producers. Growing interest in public grocery stores across Bulgaria, Canada, and places like New York City reflect an implicit understanding that workers have the right to organize, will be paid union-level wages, and food affordability will be prioritized. And for over forty years, The Landless Workers’ Movement in Brazil has actively built cross-movement solidarity by connecting rural peasants, urban workers, and international grassroots campaigns through cooperative food distribution, political education, and joint organizing.

One critical question as food prices rise is not whether workers should be paid better, but who captures value along the supply chain. Fairer food systems are about changing who holds power, who profits, and who bears the costs. This requires raising incomes, lowering the cost of living, and shifting the objective of food systems from private profit to public good, ensuring that all people can access healthy, nutritious food without depending on the exploitation of those who produce it.

The food system isn’t broken. It is working as it was designed: to use food production as a means to concentrate wealth by squeezing every penny of profit, every last drop of blood out of everyone and everything along the supply chain. Food system workers and allies can change that.
